title: MY FAVOURITE CAKE
body: A 70 year old Tehran widow, who lost her husband thirty years before and whose children have long moved abroad, is desperately lonely.  At the luncheon she organizes at home for her friends, they persuade her to go out and find a boyfriend.   In a pensioner’s cafe she overhears a conversation between an elderly divorced taxi driver and his friends.  She follows him, hires his taxi and invites him to her home.  They eat, drink home-made wine and dance.  He takes a viagra and when she joins him in the bedroom she discovers he is dead.  She buries him in the garden.  There.  No small moment of joy gets unpunished in the Islamic Republic.  Ok, there are some gently funny moments, such as when one of her friends brings along a movie to a play at the luncheon. It’s a DVD of her colonoscopy.

title: CROSSING
body: An retired schoolteacher shows up in a rundown part of Batumi, Georgia, looking for her niece, a trans sex worker.  She made a deathbed promise to her sister to find her. The niece is not there but a young man claims she is in Istanbul and that he can help find her if she takes him along.  Thus begins their odyssey through seamy neighborhoods of Istanbul looking for the absent niece.  The dour elegant schoolteacher and the handsome but somewhat unreliable youth make an odd couple. A parallel storyline follows a trans legal volunteer at an LGBT NGO in Istanbul as she negotiates the bureaucracy of her gender reclassification.  The storylines intersect when the three meet and the volunteer joins the search.  This is a very watchable movie that shines a spotlight on the difficult lives of trans women.  It reminded me somewhat of Walter Salles’ CENTRAL STATION, a favorite film of mine, but it lacks some of that movie’s epic sweep and emotional power.

title: SMALL THINGS LIKE THESE
body: A coal merchant  witnesses disturbing goings on during his regular deliveries to a local convent-run Magdelene laundry.  In these notorious nun-managed institutions, which operated in Ireland till the mid 90s, some 10’,000 young women were involuntarily institutionalised until they gave birth to babies conceived out of wedlock which which were often sold to adoptive families.  A father of five daughters, William himself is the offspring of such a union. Increasingly disturbed by the casual violence towards women in the village, he is pressured to turn a blind eye to and make a difficult moral choice.  Cillan Murphy [OPPENHEIRMER] as William, is given an opportunity to demonstrate his tremendous acting range.  Supporting actress Emely Watson [BREAKING THE WAVES] manages to project  simultaneously a convincing empathetic sweetness and a chilling terrifying determination as the convent’s mother superior.  Flemish director Tim Mielants delivers an elegant,  satisfying, though not entirely flawless drama for the Berlinale’s opening film.

title: LA COCINA
body: If you thought the restaurant kitchens portrayed in Barantini’s recent BOILING POINT or the fantastic HBO series THE CHEF were intense, they seem like meditation retreats in comparison to the one portrayed in Alonso Ruizpalacio’s LA COCINA.  When $800 goes missing from the restaurant’s cash register and the creepy owner (oddly given an Arab name but played by a heavily accented Israeli actor Oded Fehr) demands answers, the pressure is explosive.  Despite the beautiful B&W cinematography and some fine acting, the pitch is just too hysterical to be credible and the occasional philosophical ruminations tediuous.

title: YOUNG HEARTS
body: Though by no means as powerful as Lukas Dhont’s CLOSE, this tender and chaste love story of two teenage boys was certainly the kind of film I would have liked to have seen when I was of that age.  Seemed a huge crowd pleaser. Recommended.

title: ANOTHER END
body: My film festival holidays are intense and demanding.  But invariably I come across some real gems and this is one of them.  Sal [Gabriel Garcia Bernal, visibly aged though excellent] is grieving for his partner who died in a car accident for which he feels responsible.  He reluctantly is persuaded by his sister to try a new technology  that enables him to get a short period with her life consciousness [Renate Reinsve, fantastic] as therapy.  A richly layered and beautiful film about grief and longing.

title: IN LIEBE, EURE HILDE
body: The excellent 2005 film, SOPHIE SCHOLL - THE FINAL DAYS recounted the story of a member of the German resistance during WW2. Hilde Coppi,  was another such young woman.  The film starts with her arrest by the Gestapo and follows through to her eventual execution.  Her involvement in the resistance is fleshed out  through an interspersed series of regressive flashbacks.  It is an unusual narrative structure but I think it works here.  What really struck me, though, was the virtual absence of Nazi symbology or representations.  I didn’t see a Swastika until at least 30 minutes into the film, discreetly embossed on a prison guard’s helmet.  The Gestapo men taking  Hilde to be questioned  were courteous and deferential  to her pregnancy.  Even the search of her house was carried out with delicacy and respect.  This is not how you normally see Nazis in movies.   Underscoring these associations makes these oppressors seem human, universal and all the more frightening because they are so relatable.   Remarkable.

title: TREASURE
body: A holocaust survivor [the wonderful Stephen Fry] reluctantly agrees to accompany his New York journalist daughter on a road trip to Poland in 1991, as she tries to learn about their family roots.  The daughter is quite outspoken and has clearly some issues to deal with for which her father bears some responsibility.   Her abrasiveness felt quite grating initially but as she and her father come to terms with each other I developed fondness for both of them.  A gentile friend who accompanied me on this screening made an interesting comment.  He has been doing genealogical  research on Asturian immigrants to the new world.  The immigrants had a very impoverished and often never talked to their children about the lives they left behind, probably from shame or sadness.  This absence of a past was something he believed impacted these offsprings - a powerful them he could definitely relate to.

title: LOVE LIES BLEEDING
body:
A stunningly beautiful, but not too smart, bisexual bodybuilder [Katie O’Brien] hitchhikes into Louisville, Kentucky, in November 1989* and falls for the daughter [Kristen Stewart, excellent as ever] of a shady local gym owner [Ed Harris, sporting one of his most remarkable coiffures ever] and thus begins one of the sexiest, most violent, testosterone fuelled [literally], silliest and hugely entertaining movies I have seen in ages.  Recommended.

*-It’s the on the TV news, in the background.    Do they even cover foreign news on TV IN Louisville?  A wink to the Berlinale?

title: LANGUE ETRANGERE
body: A 17 year old French schoolgirl with low self esteem who pathologically lies to make herself sound more interesting finds a friend who helps her.  This delicately observed drama is bouyed by excellent performances by the two protagonists.  Highly recommended.

title: BETWEEN TWO TEMPLES
body: A middle aged cantor (who chants prayers at an upstate NY synagogue) is in a funk.  His wife has died and he is losing his voice and his faith.  His two mothers are keen to set him up with a nice girl .  While downing mudsliders (truly disgusting vodka, cream and coffee liquor cocktails) at a local bar, he gets into an altercation with a brute who has been snickering at him.  He is rescued by an older patron, his retired former music teacher.  She goes on to engage him, over her family’s objections, to prepare her for a a rather belated Bat Mitzvah ceremony.  Shot on celluloid at great speed with much improvisation by a wonderful cast working off a treatment (rather than a formal script), this charming comedy has an old fashioned American indie vibe recalling Hal Ashby’s HAROLD AND MAUD and some of the funnier moments in Cassavettes films.  Recommended.

title: DES TEUFELS BAD
body: Life in 18th century upper Austria was tough for peasant women, not least for new bride Agnes (Anja Plaschg, superb.)  She longs for a baby, but her (probably homosexual) husband is not obliging and is more interested in placating his disapproving mother.  When the psychiatric therapies offered by the local barber (don’t ask) fail to lift her depression, Agnes is driven to desperate acts.  An excellent and beautifully cinematographed film that offers some insight into the popularity of the violent medieval folk tales in Germanic cultures.

title: STERBEN
body: There is a lot going on in classical conductor Tom’s life.  His pregnant ex of 7 years wants his presence during the delivery and to help bring up the child, to the chagrin of the child’s biological father.  His terminally ill mother and demented father, living alone, are not really coping.  His composer partner is really unhappy with the piece Tom is rehearsing and is threatening to sabotage the premiere. And Tom’s sister… is a mess.  This superbly acted film, with more than a touch of dogme-style blend of humor and pathos is a bit long at 3 hours, but richly rewarding.

title: NO OTHER LAND
body: Masafer Yatta is a group of 8 villages in the occupied territories of the West Bank.  Decades ago, the area was declared a military training zone (a common occupation method of expropriation of Palestinian lands which in this case -as many - was upheld by the Israeli Supreme Court).  Since then the villagers have been caught in a cycle of demolitions/protest/illegal re-building.  Basel Adra is a local activist who five years ago was joined by Yuval Abraham, an Israeli activist journalist.  This film documents the villagers’ struggle and the Adra/Abraham collaboration.  There are some home movies of Adra’s childhood, news reports (including of a 7 minute visit by Tony Blair to Adra’s village that saved the local school) and activist footage of the demolitions and protest.  Abraham complains that few (Jewish Israelis) read his articles. Adra is increasingly tired and wondering the futility of it all.  Sadly, things have gotten only worse.  In the film’s postscript, since the October war, settlers have taken the opportunity to terrorize local villages with impunity leading many of the villagers to abandon their lands for the cities. The Palestinian terrorist attacks of the second intifada 20 years ago has alienated many Israeli Jews and worsened conditions for West Bank Palestinians.  The events of October 7th and the Israeli reaction are not harbingers of good things to come.

title: ALL SHALL BE WELL
body: Pat and Angie have been living together in the Hong Kong apartment they bought together (but is in Pat’s name) thirty years before.  At a family dinner they host we meet Pat’s brother’s family:  decent people who unfortunately have not been so lucky in life.  When Pat suddenly dies, without leaving a will, things take a predictable turn.  The narrative of gay men and women being dispossessed by the legally recognized families of the deceased partner was a common theme of LGBT cinema before gay marriage (which apparently is legally recognized but not performed in Hong Kong).  Here it is given a deft and empathetic treatment.  Recommended.

title: MAYDEGOL
body:
A ‘fly in the wall’ documentary that follows a teenager in the Islamic Republic as she pursues her passion for Thai boxing.  Unfortunately her family does not share this passion and she is the subject of physical abuse by her father (presented as sound recordings on black screen.) She takes multiple jobs to pay her club dues.  As the stateless daughter of Afghanistan refugees (her parents have lived in Iran for 50 years and cannot even buy a SIM card) she dreams of joining the Afghan 
National team.  These hopes are dashed by the victory of the Taliban.  Without papers she cannot even leave Iran legally and risks deportation to Afghanistan if caught.  If she just found an Iranian man to ‘temporarily’ marry her, she tells her friends, she would be able to travel to Turkey and thence, perhaps, America.  Grim.

title: RAIZ
body: Adolescent Feliciano with he help of his dog Rambo tends to a herd of alpacas in the highlands of Peru.  He is crazy about football and roots for Peru to qualify for the World Cup.  Unfortunately not all is idyllic in his part of the world.  The local mine is polluting the environment and Feliciano’s community is getting restless….  Feliciano and his alpacas are adorable, the landscape is gorgeous, Peru qualifies for the World Cup but the problems between the mine and the community remain unresolved.   Recommended family film.

title: REINAS
body: Lima, 1992.  The economy is in freefall, the Sendero Luminoso is terrorizing the city and anyone breaking the nightly curfew risks being shot by the army.  Travel agent Elena has secured a job in Minnesota and is desperate to take herself and her two daughters out of the country.  But first she needs to persuade the charming but no good girl’s father to sign his consent.  When, after a long absence, Carlos shows up for the elder daughter’s birthday, she and her sister are justifiably weary. This warm hearted well written, cast and directed film has justifiably won the Generation prize at the Berlinale. Highly recommended.

title: LES FANTOMES
body: Hamid, a literature professor, is a member of an underground network that seeks to bring to justice fugitive functionaries of the Assad regime hiding in Europe. Many strong moments in this film reminded me of one of my favorites, Melville’s 1969 L’ARMEE DES OMBRES, now restored and also presented at Cannes this year.  But while Melville’s film was layered with many strong, memorable characters and plot lines, this film relies almost entirely on Hamid’s pursuit and confrontation with his quarry, his prison torturer, which drags pacing at times.  Notwithstanding, Adam Bessa delivers a masterly performance as Hamid.

title: SIMON DE LA MONTAÑA
body: With facial ticks caused by psychotropic medication, 22 year old Simon is an ‘outsider.’  (Not clear if he is retarded or mentally ill. I am not certain that the actor that plays him is also disabled.) He lives in Argentina with his mum and the mum’s boyfriend for him he also works.  He and his mum have a loving relationship but it is becoming increasingly fraught.  And now with the new friends he has met at a local institution, he is getting into some trouble.  Delicately observed coming of age movie but it’s not going to have a broad appeal.

title: THE GIRL WITH THE NEEDLE
body: Copenhagen, 1918. With her husband missing in the war, a working class woman has an affair with her boss and an unwanted pregnancy. After a failed attempt to induce an abortion is a public bath, she is rescued by a kindly sweet-shop owner who has a side business trafficking babies.  An engaging, though at times harrowing, worthy competitor for le palme d’or. Recommended. <This message was edited>

title: LOCUST
body: Routine drama about a mute Taipei dishwasher that moonlights in a violent debt collection gang.  The Hong Kong protests seen on TV screens in the background and the solidarity demonstrations in Taipei feel like a forced attempt to add some relevance for western art house audiences. Not recommended. <This message was edited>

title: BIRD
body: Andrea Arnold (FISH TANK) returns with another searing portrait of childhood in a British housing estate.  This time we follow 12 year old Bailey as she tries to manage the pressures of her own burgeoning adolescence while looking out for her neglected younger siblings.  Barry Kehogan (SALTBURN) is excellent as the loving but irresponsible dad, and the wonderful Franz Rugowski (GREAT FREEDOM, LUBO) is superbly cast as Bird, the enigmatic friend Bailey meets in the fields.  Highly recommended. <This message was edited>

title: MEGALOPOLIS
body: I sat through the entire 138 minutes of this film out of respect for this veteran filmmaker.  Yes, there were some glimpses of his cinematic brilliance in some scenes, but mostly this felt like a hot mess:  stylistically dated, annoying and pretentious.

title: RENDEZ-VOUS AVEC POT
body: A French Communist writer, a photojournalist and a radio-journalist land in Khmer Rouge controlled Cambodia in 1975 as guests of the regime.  While the writer, who attended the Sorbonne with Pol Pot and  some of his colleagues is broadly sympathetic to the revolutionaries, the other two are more skeptical of what they are shown.  The photojournalist evades his hosts to document the famine gripping the country and disappears.  The naivite and hypocrisy of the writer gradually becomes evident. The interesting themes explored in this movie are let down by the low budget filmmaking that takes place almost entirely in a deserted airfield and relies on newsreel footage and animated dioramas to illustrate the narrative. Passable. <This message was edited>

title: LA BELLE DU GAZA
body:
Yolanda Zauberman’s last documentary, M, with its sea-sickness inducing out of focus hand held camerawork was as messy as its subject, a sexual abuse survivor in the Jewish ultra orthodox community. 
I am sad to report that Zauberman’s hand has not become any steadier nor has her focus-pulling ability improved however her affectionate portrait of four courageous Arab trans women (and one Jewish mama) in Tel Aviv merits a viewing.

title: KINDS OF KINDNESS
body: A lot has been said elsewhere about the new Yorgos Lanthimos triptych of fables, all more or less with the same cast, set in a Ballardian New Orleans.  Suffice to say that I never liked any of his films and I did not feel differently about this one.

title: OH, CANADA
body: Paul Schrader’s own reported poor health makes the theme of his film about a dying documentary filmmaker giving a last interview, that feels very much like a confession, in front of his wife, quite apt. Schrader’s films always struck me as being highly influenced by his Christianity, and this film is no exception. Richard Gere and Jacob Elordi alternate play the young antihero (think Buñuel THAT OBSCURE OBJECT OF DESIRE).  Very watchable.

title: THE SHAMELESS
body: This drama about the seamy underbelly of Indian life is given a masterly treatment in Konstantin Bojanov’s gripping film about two sex workers who fall for each other.  Omara Shetty and Aurashika Dey deliver absolutely astounding performances. Highly recommended.

title: MOST PEOPLE DIE ON SUNDAYS
body: A charming low-key comedy about a 30 year old emotionally immature Jewish gay man who returns to his native Buenos Aires for his uncle’s funeral.  Very much in the style of American independent films of an earlier era. Very watchable.

title: EMILIA PÉREZ
body: A musical about a Mexican drug kingpin who is seeking to change his life through a discreet gender reassignment surgery?  Musicals are not my favorite genre. As someone well aware of the tremendous human cost the crime epidemic that sweeps Mexico, I was also weary of anyone trying to make light entertainment of it.  But EMILIA PEREZ floored me.  It was deeply moving, often surprising and with a wonderful score. Very highly recommended.

title: LIMONOV - THE BALLAD
body: Eduard Limonov was a Russian poet, writer, dissident and politician.  He was ‘encouraged’ to emigrate during Soviet times, lead a very colourful life in New York in the 70s, formed an ultra Nationalist Russian political party on his return after the fall of the USSR for which he was rewarded with a stint in Siberian prison camp.  (Many of his followers volunteered to fight with Donebas separatists. Limonov died in 2020).  Ben Wishaw delivers a tour de force performance in this visually impressive film.

title: ARMAND
body: A 6-year old child has been found in a school bathroom by the cleaner, bruised and with his pants down, has accused a friend of attacking him.  Parents are summoned by school officials for an investigation and their confrontation is the core of this film.  But what starts out as a chamber piece takes some weird surreal/metaphorical turns before a delivering a satisfying and conventional resolution to the drama. I liked this film but it did make me think of Ilker Çatak’s excellent 2023 THE TEACHER’S LOUNGE, a similar themed film that I very much prefer. Last year’s film is currently on general release in the UK.

title: BLUE SUN PALACE
body: A Taiwanese immigrant, his wife and daughter back home, tries to escape his loneliness by dating another immigrant who works in a grubby massage parlor in Queens, New York (but it could be anywhere, even Gijon!)  When she dies in a tragic incident, he begins to to court her friend and colleague at the parlor.  Some people really like this low key film. I found it boring and depressing in equal measure. Sorry.

title: THE SUBSTANCE
body: In this odd choice for Palme D’Or competition, Demi Moore plays a has been Hollywood star.  The producer on her remaining gig, an aerobic workout tv show (a la Jane Fonda’s workout videos of the nineties) is advertising for her replacement.  She is offered the opportunity to undertake a subscription based medical treatment that promises a new improved self.  Like Ozempic it works, but there are some unintended consequences…. It must have taken some real balls (or desperation) for Moore to accept a role that exposes her aging body in such a brutal way.  While the premise of the film is interesting and for the most part it is very entertaining, it suffers the fate of most films of this genre by taking things too far. <This message was edited>

title: THREE KILOMETERS TO THE END OF THE WORLD
body: Adi has returned to stay with his parents for the summer in Romania’s Danube Delta.  On his way home one evening he is brutally assaulted.  The police soon finds the culprits, a couple of thugs and the motive - gay bashing.  The beating soon turns out to be the least of Adi’s problems as it is in everyone’s interest for the problem to ‘go away’ and for Adi to be cured of his affliction.  A deft and tightly executed drama. Highly recommended. <This message was edited>

title: THE APPRENTICE
body: THE APPRENTICE was the name Of Donald Trump’s TV show. But in in Ali Abbasi’s film, the apprentice is Donald Trump himself.  In the 1970s, when he was going door to door collecting rents for his dad, Trump met Roy Cohn, the notorious NYC lawyer. From him he learns the ruthlessness and vile needed to achieve what he has.  The first assignment, getting rid of a federal prosecution against discriminatory rental practices in Trump’s properties, is resolved by blackmailing the prosecutor’s boss.  The film ends with Cohn at his deathbed, getting one last call from Trump asking for some free legal advice.  Sebastian Stang and Jeremy Strong are convincing as Trump and Cohn respectively.  Like LIMONOV, reviewed yesterday, this gripping film borrows a strong visual style from the period, occasionally blending contemporaneous TV footage. Recommended.

title: BABY
body:
Baby is Wellington, an 18 year old gay youth released from a juvenile institution to find that his parents left Sao Paolo without leaving a forwarding address.  After a night in the streets he joins some friends, queer and trans sex workers in robbing patrons in a porn cinema.  It is there that Baby is attracted to Marcelo, a sex worker more than twice his age. While reticent at first, Marcelo soon takes Baby under his wing and mentors him on his trade. When Marcelo becomes jealous of Baby’s assertions of his own autonomy, Baby leaves him for an older middle class man and moves in with him. A chance encounter in the street with a fellow inmate spells an end to that romance as Baby’s new lover was unaware of his criminal past. He returns to Marcelo and gets entangled in his drug dealing sideline and is almost killed.  Baby then returns to his queer gang that now vogue-dance on public busses for handouts.  

While most directors would choose to
portray Baby as a tragic victim,  in this film he appears to be much in control of his life and able to find pleasure and happiness despite his circumstances.  Recommended.

title: ANORA
body:
Russian-speaking Ani performs lap dances  in a New York strip club. Occasionally, she is accepts escort gigs such as from Vanya, the young son of an oligarch whom she meets there.  He really likes her and she seems to enjoy her time either him so she does not hesitate in accepting his offer to hire her as his ‘girlfriend’ for a week.  He soon whisks her and some young friends to Vegas for wild break.  It is there that he proposes to her and they get married before returning to New York.  News of the union soon reaches Vanya’s parents in Moscow prompting a frenzied effort to annul the marriage. 

Sean Baker is a master cinematic storyteller, expertly blending comedy and pathos and is supported by superb performances by the three leads. Highly recommended. <This message was edited>

title: PARTHENOPE
body: You either love Paolo Sorrentino’s films or you don’t.  If long languid tracking shots of beautiful (or grotesque) people, expensively dressed, against stunning Mediterranean landscapes, smoking cigarettes as they plunge into the sea or swimming pools are your thing, then you will find plenty to like here.  We follow the life of Parthenope, a beautiful and clever anthropology professor from her birth, through the suicide of her brother, to her retirement in the present day.  Garry Oldman makes an odd, pointless, cameo as the writer John Cheever. I guess he is one of the grotesques. <This message was edited>

title: GRAND TOUR
body: Second competition film I walked out on today. In 1917 a British colonial officer flees Rangoon just as his fiancée of 7 years is about to join him.  His ‘grand tour’ takes him across Asia, filmed in the present day in alternating colour and monochrome (without apparent significance) with voiceovers in Thai, Malay, Japanese etcétera narrate his journey. When he speaks, it is in Portuguese. One wonders how films are selected for the competition. <This message was edited>

title: BEING MARIA
body:
When Maria Schneider’s mother learns that her 16 year old daughter has gone out to lunch with her estranged husband (and Maria’s father), the actor Daniel Gelin, she kicks her out of their home.  Maria turns to her father’s agent and is soon offered a role in Bertolucci’s LAST TANGO IN PARIS. The Director is looking for “a blank page”, he tells her, to play alongside Marlon Brando.  In a pivotal scene, Brando, at Bertolucci’s direction, goes off script and rapes Schneider.  

Despite her assertions in the media that she did not consent to the scene, Schneider is denigrated for her participation and convicted in Italy, alongside the two men, for obscenity.  Moreover the roles she is subsequently offered  typecast her as a quasi pornographic actress.  She becomes a heroin addict, which over the years also causes difficulties with her lesbian lover.  

Anamaria Vartolomei is superb as Schneider  as is Matt Dillon as Brando. Jessica Palud directs with confidence and verve. Highly recommended. <This message was edited>

title: L’HISTORIE DE SOULEYMANE
body: This powerful and timely drama follows Souleymane during the two days prior to his asylum request interview in Paris.  He visits his ‘interview coach’, whom he has engaged to fabricate a false asylum claim. He supports himself illegally by cycling and delivering meals using credentials rented from someone else and sleeps in homeless shelters.  As expected, the interview falls apart and the truth emerges.  The cast, headed by Abou Sangare, is very convincing.  Recommended. <This message was edited>

title: SPECTATEURS!
body: In this intimate cinematic essay, Arnaud Desplechin ruminates about cinema.  He combines dramatized sequences from his life (first visit to the cinema with his grandmother, his film club screenings in secondary school, university lectures he found significant), clips from movies he likes, interviews with cineastes and critics he admires and with cinema goers about their habits and preferences.  As I increasingly find myself attending almost empty theatres (outside of festivals) I fear we might soon lose the wonderful shared experience of going to the movies.

title: THE SHROUDS
body: Cronenberg’s competition contestant has a man so much in grief for his dead wife that his teeth begin to rot, according to his dentist. He develops a franchise of cemeteries where bodies are interred with a high tech shroud (designed by co producer Saint Laurent) that enables their relatives to view their bodies disintegrate in real time via an app.  Unlike the other body horror competition contestant, THE SUBSTANCE, this one cannot even be accused of being entertaining.  The plot is so convoluted that even SCREEN DAILY, which dosing critics rely on to fill in the gaps they have missed, gave up on this one.  Not recommended.

title: VIET  AND NAM
body: In almost every major festival these days you get at least one exotic third world gay romance.  These films are almost never shown in their home countries but are destined for LGBT+ film festivals and boutique streaming platforms.  I don’t think you can get much more exotic than two Vietnamese miners who copulate only while in the mines.  Above ground they discuss the desire of one of them to emigrate and help the mother and uncle to look for the body of one of their fathers who died in the war.  Extremely dull.

title: NASTY - MORE THAN JUST TENNIS
body: Documentary on the first bad boy of tennis, Ilie Nastasie.  Probably more than I wanted to know about the man, but quite watchable. HBO co-produced so expect on Sky in the UK.

title: TO LIVE, TO DIE, TO LIVE AGAIN
body:
Emma knows her partner and father of their child Sammy is bisexual but is willing to accept that as long as he does not leave her.  Her attitude changes when, in 1990, she discovers his affair with next door neighbor, fine art photographer Cyril and worse yet when she learns that Sammy has full blown AIDS and that she too is infected.  (Cyril is HIV positive and is unable to tolerate AZT, but it appears that Sammy acquired his infection before they met.) As Cyril’s own health deteriorates, he decides to marry Emma so she could benefit from his inheritance (France’s Napoleonic code predetermines beneficiaries).  They all go on a honeymoon to a beautiful villa in Italy lent to them by Cyril’s gallery owner.  Sammy unfortunately dies soon afterwards.  Five years later, both Cyril and Emma have responded well to the triple therapy cocktail. With his newly acquired health, Cyril loses his artistic drive. Emma, seeking to end her dependence on Cyril, divorces him.  She organizes one last show of Cyril’s photographs of Sammy.

Everyone looks beautiful and adorable in Gaël Morel’s film (Victor Belmondo has an uncanny resemblance to his dad,) even though they always seem to wear exactly the same underwear over the years. But that does not stop it feeling unconvincing and inauthentic. And it is not helped by the soppy score.  Pass.

title: MOTEL DESTINO
body: A young hitman on the run is holed up in a steamy love motel (one that offers ‘premium fucking’, no less, according to the motel’s owner.) He falls for the owner’s wife who proposes they kill her husband… The somewhat intensified color palette, as if shot on Kodachrome, provides a punch to this tropical noir. Recommended. <This message was edited>

title: ALL WE IMAGINE AS LIGHT
body: Prabha is a nurse at a Mumbai hospital. Her husband had left to work in Germany and she had not heard from him in over a year. Her roommate Anu, a junior nurse, has a secret Moslem boyfriend. Meanwhile another friend, a hospital cook, is facing eviction from her apartment by developers.  A delicately observed, gentle paced drama about female friendship. Recommended.

title: THE SEED OF THE SACRED FIG
body:
Iman has just been promoted as an investigating magistrate, a short stepping stone to judgeship on Iran’s revolutionary courts.  His wife and daughters are delighted given the prospect of elevated lifestyle and especially of being able to move to a larger apartment.  Unfortunately, the courts are unpopular and their functionaries have to be discreet lest they are targeted by the regime’s enemies, so Amin is issued with a gun.  Also some moral qualms are keeping Amin awake at night.  His predecessor was fired because he refused to greenlight a prosecution that carries the death penalty.  But then again, the prosecutor that cannot be refused is insisting and anyway there are appeals procedures to deal with any miscarriages of justice later down the line.  And also Amin’s wife would really like a dishwasher.  
Soon, however, Iran is engulfed by the Mahsa Amini protests which impacts the girls in school and university. The jails are filling up and death sentences are handed out like candy on Halloween.  And then Amin’s gun goes missing. 

Despite its almost three hour length, Mohammad Rasoulof urgent, courageous and timely picture kept me at the edge of my seat. Highly recommended. <This message was edited>

title: THE MOST PRECIOUS CARGO
body:
A baby girl is thrown off a train in the dead of winter. The poor woodcutter’s wife who picks her up thinks she is the answer to her prayers.  Her husband is less than thrilled, rightfully suspecting that the baby belongs to a cursed race. When his wife refuses to surrender the baby, he banishes the two to the woodshed for the rest of the winter.  I don’t think it’s too much of a spoiler to say that he eventually changes his attitude. The rest I will leave for you to discover.
This elegantly drawn animation pic is not really for children despite its occasional sentimental appeal.  Recommended.

title: NONOSTANTE
body: Dreary romantic comedy set in a large Italian hospital.  The three dour-faced characters roaming the halls, ignored by the nurses and doctors, initially seem like underemployed administrators.  Turns out they are actually ghosts there to facilitate the transition of the souls of the comatose and dying hospital residents.  The patients apparently can leave their bodies to join the ghosts in their wanderings. One of the ghosts is attracted to one of the patients.  How will their romance pan out?  I didn’t stay to find out.  Passable.

title: A QUIET LIFE
body: Worthy but flawed immigration drama.  Yuri, a dissident headmaster from Russia, flees to Sweden with his family after an attack by police and FSB officers. His asylum application is rejected due to lack of corroborating evidence. The only witness was his younger daughter. He had initially prevented her from testifying as it might cause her to relive the trauma.  However, faced with impending deportation, he asks her to appear before the appeals board. Days before the hearing, the daughter lapses into a comatose ‘resignation syndrome’: a condition afflicting hundreds of children of asylum seekers in Sweden, according to the end credits. Bouyed by some really strong central performances, the film’s credibility is unfortunately undermined by overstylised set pieces and some cartoonish secondary characters. The lower key recent Cannes award winner, L’HISTORIE DE SOULEMAYNE, dealt with similar themes more convincingly. <This message was edited>

title: SEPTEMBER 5
body: The 1972 Munich Olympics were the first to gain live satellite TV coverage. Peter Sarsgaard, a sports TV producer for ABC finds himself thrust into a newsroom crisis when Black September terrorists take the Israeli team hostage in the Olympic village.  It is striking that in these days when anyone can broadcast their own facts and opinions (‘alternative’ or not) the trouble these sport journalists took to confirm and reconfirm the floating rumors in the midst of the chaos and confusion. Even then they got things wrong.  It turned out to be the most watched TV coverage in history to that point and a milestone in the weaponisation of world media attention by terrorist groups.  Watchable but not great. <This message was edited>

title: EL JOCKEY (KILL THE JOCKEY)
body: It would not occur to me to cast the wonderful Nahuel Pérez Biscayet (120 BPM) in a comic role.  Yet with his large sad eyes and delicate vulnerability he does bear more than a passing resemblance to Buster Keaton.  Here he plays a drug addicted Buenos Aires jockey who upsets his gangster sponsor by failing to win a race.  This film has its memorable moments but did not really appeal to me.

title: SEPARATED
body: Trump’s zero tolerance immigration policy used forced separation of parents from their children who were captured after illegally crossing the border as a way to dissuade others from attempting it.  Bowing to domestic and international outrage, Trump eventually rescinded the policy but not before over 4,000 children and babies were subjected to it.   Of them about a quarter have still not been reunited: in effect state created orphans.  In this superb documentary, Errol Morris (THE THIN BLUE LINE, THE FOG OF WAR) exposes not only the cruelty of these who conceived of this policy but also how some grey and ambitious political appointees became complicit in its implementation.  Trump has not ruled out using this method again if re-elected. It’s tough but it works, he says. The one thing that could prevent it is legislation from Congress which has failed to act. With hate of immigrants so deeply fanned over the years, one of Morris’s interviewees wonders if the American public has not become too desensitized to protest if such policies were reintroduced by his next  administration. <This message was edited>

title: RIEFENSTAHL
body: The extensive clips from her work as a filmmaker and photographer (and to a lesser extent as an actress) presented in this fascinating documentary confirm Leni Rifenstahl’s vast talent.  Like her close friend, the architect and Nazi munitions minister Albert Speer, she spent much of the postwar period defending and monetizing her reputation.  Despite her often angry protestations in many TV and film interviews that she did not know of the war crimes nor that she was a complicit propagandist for the Nazi regime, ample evidence is provided here to the contrary.  “What disappearances,” she asks one interviewer, “all my Jewish friends left before the war. Even my doctor left for America.”  The filmmakers present a rich trove of material, much of it previously unseen, from her estate.  One particularly shocking incident is striking.  Covering the German campaign in Poland, Riefenstahl was in a town filming some Warmacht soldiers.  In the foreground there were some Jews digging a ditch. Thinking that the composition is unsightly, she asked the commandant “to have the Jews removed.” The commandant took this stage direction to mean that the Jews should be summarily executed. In a still image we see Riefenstahl’s horrified reaction. She decided to abandon her war correspondent role and returned to Berlin to film one of Hitler’s favorite operettas.  Essential viewing.

title: BABYGIRL
body: Romy (Kidman) is a high powered executive happily married for 19 years to theatre director Jacob (Banderas) and they have two lovely daughters. Everything is almost perfect except that Romy has submission fantasies that Jacob cannot oblige.  Enter Samuel (Dickinson), a cocky New York intern who has a way of taming wild dogs and women…  While the foregoing sounds like a  cheesy morality play, with a predictable ending where lust will go rightfully punished, it isn’t.  Gently comic, it is superbly written and acted and actually quite sexy.  Even Kidman allows a gentle joke at her expense. “You look weird mum, like a dead fish,” her lesbian daughter tells her, after Romy gets her Botox injections. Highly recommended.

title: DICIANNOVE
body: 19 year old Leonardo is a literature student, vegetarian, gay, depressed, has nosebleeds, hates his professor.  Not sure what was keeping the entire audience at the massive Sala Dársena glued to their seats but I left after an hour.

title: MARCO
body: Some 9000 Spaniards ended up in Nazi concentration camps, most were Republicans who spent the previous years in French internment camps. After the war many could not return to Spain. Between 2001 and 2005, Enric Marco headed an association of former deportees who fought for recognition from the Spanish government. Just as the then President Zapatero agreed to go to Malthausen concentration camp for a commemoration event, it emerged that Marco was a fraud.  He was in Germany during the war, but went as a volunteer to work in their munitions factories.  This film follows Marco as he conceives and executes his deceit, how it is  undone by a historian and the years he spent trying to reframe his ‘legacy’. It is a compelling, well told and acted tale.  Yet I was disturbed by how we are fascinated and give attention to fraudsters and charlatans while the stories of the real victims are often left untold.

title: AINDA ESTOU AQUÍ
body:
Eunice lives a comfortable middle class life with her five children and civil engineer husband Bruno in their house by the beach in Rio. It is 1970 and the country is ruled by a military dictatorship.  One day, armed, unidentified men show up at their home and take Bruno away. 

There have been other films about political disappearances in Latin America. Some of them like this one, focus on the impact on families. Based on a true story, this unsensational, delicately observed telling from Walter Salles [CENTRAL STATION] is exceptional in conveying the unsettling nature of Eunice’s experience.  Fernanda Torres delivers a stunning performance as a woman whose courage, humour and fortitude are truly inspiring.

title: FROM DARKNESS TO LIGHT
body:
In 1972, 15 years before Begnini made LIFE IS BEAUTIFUL, Jerry Lewis tried to make a Holocaust comedy in Sweden. [Mel Brooks’ made THE PRODUCERS in 1967, but that was a comedy about Nazis, not concentration camps. Interviewed here, Brooks was aghast at the idea.]. Lewis’s film was never finished. The main producer withdrew in the middle of the shoot. Worse yet, he let the the option for the rights to the works to lapse. The writer did not like the work Jerry Lewis showed him and refused to sell them.  The production facilities company held the reels of the film hostage pending payment that never came. Former employees there surreptitiously salvaged the reels when that company went bust.  This film presents extensive clips from the salvaged rough cut, together with a long interview with Lewis a few years before he died. There are also interviews with collaborators and fans including a very generous Martin Scorsese. 

The film that Lewis tried to make was THE DAY THE CLIWN CRIED. It was about a circus clown, sent to a concentration camp over a drunken outburst about Hitler. There he is asked to amuse Jewish children as they are led to the gas chambers.

It was not a good time in Lewis’s life.  His recent films flopped. He was heavily invested in a cinema franchising business that failed as well.  He had troubles with the mostly Swedish cast.  In the interview Lewis says he did not like his work on this film and I have to agree, most of it is really bad.  

Shaken by the experience, Lewis retreated to Las Vegas and did not appear in any films for over a decade, until what is probably his best:  Scorsese’s KING OF COMEDY.

title: THE ROOM NEXT DOOR
body:
Ingrid (Moore), in New York for a book signing, reconnects after years with her old friend Marta (Swinton).  The war correspondent is in hospital with inoperable cervical cancer. After leaving the hospital, in a break from her treatments, Martha confides to Ingrid that she intends to end her life. She wants Ingrid to be with her when she does this, in the room next door.

After the slightly awkward initial scenes in which, in Sirkian style, the characters set out their backstories, the lusciously filmed drama soon takes on a more naturalistic rhythm. Both Swinton and Moore are terrific. Recommended.

title: FAMILIA
body: A familiar tale of a wife beating husband, his traumatized wife and sons and the incompetence of the authorities to deal with it effectively - with predictable results. Watchable, but not great.

title: THE BRUTALIST
body: In this 215m epic, Laszlo Toth, a Bahuaus trained Jewish Hungarian architect and camp survivor, tries to reprise his career in America while he waits for his wife and niece to rejoin him from Europe.  It features impressive performances by Adrien Brody and Guy Pearce as the wealthy American patron who commissions him to construct a monumental project.  The film offers a rich and nuanced exploration of the outsider immigrant experience and the fraught interaction between artistic genius and capital.  Demanding but rewarding viewing.

title: QUEER
body: IWilliam Burroughs’s autobiographical novel QUEER, about his time in Mexico City in the late fourties and his affair with a discharged American serviceman with whom he travels to South America, is exquisitely honest and melancholic.  Luca Guadagnino’s adaptation, with its stunning production design retains some of the novel’s tone but layers impressionistic/surreal touches that pay tribute to the writer’s other works. It would have never occurred to me to offer the role of Burroughs to Daniel Craig [007] but both he and Drew Starkey are very good.

title: JOUER AVEC LE FEU
body: Vincent Lindon plays a railway worker bringing up two teenage sons in a northern french town. His elder son becomes  involved  with a far right group and kills an anti-fascist activist.  If the plot sounds familiar you may be remembering Bernard Tavernier’s excellent 1974 film L’HOROLOGER DE ST PAUL.  Both films focus on the father’s reaction to the political murder by their son.  But whereas Lindon’s character is repelled and is ashamed of his son’s actions, Noiret’s was broadly supportive and proud.  This film is ok but If we are going to make comparisons, Tavernier’s  left a stronger impression on me. <This message was edited>

title: DIVA FUTURA
body: The adventures of Ricardo Schicchi, the producer who ‘discovered’ Ilona Staller (aka Cicciolina) and Moana Pozzi.  Strictly for Italian soft core porn nostalgia aficionados. Co produced with Netflix.

title: FAMILIAR TOUCH
body: Ruth, now in her seventies, is entertaining a gentleman for lunch. He is an architect, she finds out, but also disappointingly married. When this doesn’t stop her from gently flirting with him he tells her that they need to get going. The gentleman is her son, who has come to take his memory-impaired mother to a nursing home.  Thus begins one of the small gems of the festival: a beautifully observed coming of (old) age movie, which with pathos and humor follows Ruth as she adjusts to her new life.  Very highly recommended American indie.

title: SHAHED
body: Below average Iranian feminist drama. A Tehran dance teacher is murdered by her abusive, regime-connected husband.  The murder is witnessed by her godmother, the head of the teachers’ union.  Predictably, the efforts of the witness to bring the culprit to justice are frustrated by the authorities.  In a clumsy cinematic metaphor, the witness’s apartment is infested with vermin.

title: AL KLAVIM VEANASHIM
body:
A month after the October 7 attack by Hamas, Dar, an internally displaced teenager sneaks back to Kibbutz Nir Oz, now a restricted military area, looking to rescue Shula, the dog she left behind.  Dar had hidden under the bed when the Hamas terrorists entered their home and kidnapped her mother.  Amidst the ruins of the burnt out Kibbutz, Dar encounters Nathan, a lone elderly neighbour who decided to stay, the kindergarten teacher looking to bring back some toys and games to the displaced children, forensic workers collecting body parts and a couple of animal rescuers. Occasionally, there are alert sirens and Hamas rockets land in the kibbutz. In the distance, Israeli bombers attack Gaza.  While sheltering from the rockets, Dar flicks on her phone through Hamas videos of their attack and scenes of the devastation in Gaza.  A particularly poignant animated sequence imagines Shula chasing after the Hamas pick up van taking Dar’s mother away and befriending and being sheltered by a young Palestinian boy amidst the Israeli bombing.  

Like in Dani Rosenberg’s previous film, the wonderful ON DEATH OF THE CINEMA AND MY FATHER TOO, which premiered in Venice last year, most of  the characters (all except  Dar in this film) play themselves. The film was shot in the kibbutz in November last year.  The tone is sombre, but empathetic to the senseless suffering on both sides of the border.  There was a petition to withdraw the invitation of the film from the festival. It would have been a shame if it succeeded.

title: ANORA
body:
Russian-speaking Ani performs lap dances  in a New York strip club. Occasionally, she is accepts escort gigs such as from Vanya, the young son of an oligarch whom she meets there.  He really likes her and she seems to enjoy her time with him so she does not hesitate in accepting his offer to hire her as his ‘girlfriend’ for a week.  He soon whisks her and some young friends to Vegas for wild break.  It is there that he proposes to her and they get married before returning to New York.  News of the union soon reaches Vanya’s parents in Moscow prompting a frenzied effort to annul the marriage. 

Sean Baker is a master cinematic storyteller, expertly blending comedy and pathos and is supported by superb performances by the three leads. Highly recommended.

title: THE APPRENTICE
body: THE APPRENTICE was the name Of Donald Trump’s TV show. But in in Ali Abbasi’s film, the apprentice is Donald Trump himself.  In the 1970s, when he was going door to door collecting rents for his dad, Trump met Roy Cohn, the notorious NYC lawyer. From him he learns the ruthlessness and vile needed to achieve what he has.  The first assignment, getting rid of a federal prosecution against discriminatory rental practices in Trump’s properties, is resolved by blackmailing the prosecutor’s boss.  The film ends with Cohn at his deathbed, getting one last call from Trump asking for some free legal advice.  Sebastian Stang and Jeremy Strong are convincing as Trump and Cohn respectively.  Like LIMONOV, reviewed yesterday, this gripping film borrows a strong visual style from the period, occasionally blending contemporaneous TV footage. Recommended.

title: EMILIA PÉREZ
body: A musical about a Mexican drug kingpin who is seeking to change his life through a discreet gender reassignment surgery?  Musicals are not my favorite genre. As someone well aware of the tremendous human cost the crime epidemic that sweeps Mexico, I was also weary of anyone trying to make light entertainment of it.  But EMILIA PEREZ floored me.  It was deeply moving, often surprising and with a wonderful score. Very highly recommended.

After leaving the hospital, in a break from her treatments, Martha confides to Ingrid that she intends to end her life. She wants Ingrid to be with her when she does this, in the room next door.

After the slightly awkward initial scenes in which, in Sirkian style, the characters set out their backstories, the lusciously filmed drama soon takes on a more naturalistic rhythm. Both Swinton and Moore are terrific. Recommended.

title: ALL WE IMAGINE AS LIGHT
body: Prabha is a nurse at a Mumbai hospital. Her husband had left to work in Germany and she had not heard from him in over a year. Her roommate Anu, a junior nurse, has a secret Moslem boyfriend. Meanwhile another friend, a hospital cook, is facing eviction from her apartment by developers.  A delicately observed, gentle paced drama about female friendship. Recommended.

title: THE SEED OF THE SACRED FIG
body:
Iman has just been promoted as an investigating magistrate, a short stepping stone to judgeship on Iran’s revolutionary courts.  His wife and daughters are delighted given the prospect of elevated lifestyle and especially of being able to move to a larger apartment.  Unfortunately, the courts are unpopular and their functionaries have to be discreet lest they are targeted by the regime’s enemies, so Amin is issued with a gun.  Also some moral qualms are keeping Amin awake at night.  His predecessor was fired because he refused to greenlight a prosecution that carries the death penalty.  But then again, the prosecutor that cannot be refused is insisting and anyway there are appeals procedures to deal with any miscarriages of justice later down the line.  And also Amin’s wife would really like a dishwasher.  
Soon, however, Iran is engulfed by the Mahsa Amini protests which impacts the girls in school and university. The jails are filling up and death sentences are handed out like candy on Halloween.  And then Amin’s gun goes missing. 

Despite its almost three hour length, Mohammad Rasoulof urgent, courageous and timely picture kept me at the edge of my seat. Highly recommended.

title: ALL SHALL BE WELL
body: Pat and Angie have been living together in the Hong Kong apartment they bought together (but is in Pat’s name) thirty years before.  At a family dinner they host we meet Pat’s brother’s family:  decent people who unfortunately have not been so lucky in life.  When Pat suddenly dies, without leaving a will, things take a predictable turn.  The narrative of gay men and women being dispossessed by the legally recognized families of the deceased partner was a common theme of LGBT cinema before gay marriage (which apparently is legally recognized but not performed in Hong Kong).  Here it is given a deft and empathetic treatment.  Recommended.

title: THREE KILOMETERS TO THE END OF THE WORLD
body: Adi has returned to stay with his parents for the summer in Romania’s Danube Delta.  On his way home one evening he is brutally assaulted.  The police soon finds the culprits, a couple of thugs and the motive - gay bashing.  The beating soon turns out to be the least of Adi’s problems as it is in everyone’s interest for the problem to ‘go away’ and for Adi to be cured of his affliction.  A deft and tightly executed drama. Highly recommended.

title: HOME 2
body: I will he presenting this film at the Phoenix cinema in north London.  It is based on a true story and highlights one of the more serious fault lines in modern Israeli society.

title: WELCOME HOME BABY
body: In this cliché laden horror pic, a Berlin emergency room doctor travels to a small Austrian village where she inherited a house from a biological father she did not know.  In short order she finds herself coddled by the town’s creepy woman folk and an unwanted pregnancy.  With more than a nod to Polanski’s ROSEMARY’S BABY (even Julia Franz Richter has more than a passing resemblance to Mia Farrow) this film is redeemed by neither humour nor originality. Odd choice for the opening film of the Panorama section.

title: PETER HUJAR’S DAY
body: After starring in his 2023 PASSAGES, Ben Wishaw returns, this time alongside Rebecca Hall, to work with Ira Sachs on this film: a dramatization of a 1971 interview given by New York photographer Peter Hujar, to writer Linda Rosenkrantz.  For 75 minutes the chainsmoking Hujar tells Rosenkrantz what he did the previous day.  Yup, that’s it!  Even for this fan of Ben Wishaw, these 75 minutes felt really long.

title: ARI
body: Ari, a trainee primary school teacher, suffers a nervous breakdown during a class  inspection.  His father is appalled by his subsequent decision to quit his profession and kicks him out of his home.  For the rest of the film we follow Ari as he drifts around between his friends who, he discovers, are just as fucked up as he is.  While the initial scenes at school and with his dad are deftly drawn and truly comic, it is evident that the success of this film depends on it’s ability to generate audience sympathy and empathy for Ari and his friends.  Unfortunately, at least with this audience member (and I suspect many others), this film failed.

title: MICKEY 17
body: The bug buzz in Berlin this year is about Korean director Bong Jon Ho’s [PARASITE] first English language sci fi film.  Marc Ruffalo plays a character styled on a blend of Elon Musk and Donald Trump who sets out on an expedition to colonize a distant planet.  He receives a special dispensation to employ a technology considered too risky for earth:  the ability to digitally re-print humans that retain the memories of the originals. One might criticize Ruffalo for hamming it up a bit. His character is a bit of a caricature but on reflection the originals it is based on seem just as scarily ridiculous.  Did I like it?  The film felt a little too optimistic for me. (Spoiler:  The Ruffalo character implodes as does the offending technology.) But perhaps optimism is what we need!

title: CICADAS
body: Veteran actress Nina Haas and Saskia Rosendahl deliver outstanding performances in this film about a friendship between two women.  Childless Isabell’s marriage is on the rocks and she has difficulty finding care for her two elderly parents.  Meanwhile single mother Anja (Rosendahl) is struggling to keep jobs while looking after her young daughter.  Eventually their lives intersect and a bond develops between them.  Eventually, Isabell hires Anja to help care for her parents.  An unexpected  climatic development leaves Isabell and the audience puzzled.  Slow burning but very watchable.

title: DREAMS
body:
ballet dancer Fernando sneaks across the border illegally to join Jennifer in San Francisco.  The two had a brief but torrid affair in Mexico City where they met when Jennifer was there to oversee the dance school her foundation supports.  Jennifer is pleased to see Fernando. When, after a few days, it becomes evident to him that she is embarrassed to be seen in his presence, he leaves.  Jennifer obsessively pursues him until he relents and they resume their relationship. Fernando joins the San Francisco ballet company and is offered a teaching post there.  One day, ICE shows up at the school and Fernando is deported.  While Jennifer follows him to Mexico City it does not end well for either of them.
Achingly handsome Isaac Hernandez (Fernando) and the older but also beautiful Jessica Chastain (Jennifer) deliver powerful performances in this nuanced and delicately observed drama about a passionate but power imbalanced relationship. Highly recommended. <This message was edited>

title: HOUSES
body: Sasha, young and non binary, revisits old abandoned childhood homes and reviews creepy childhood videos captured by their abusive father while occasionally taking calls from their oblivious mother.  I left as tortured by watching this dull movie as Sasha’s soul.  Give it a pass.

title: HOLDING LIAT
body: History teacher Liat and her husband Aviv were kidnapped from their home in Nir Oz on October 7th.  Almost immediately filmmaker and distant relative Brandon Kramer started documenting her family’s efforts to get her released.  (Aviv, we later discover, was killed.)  Unlike the other Berlinale Israeli October 7th doc, MICHTAV LE’DAVID that focused on the personal tragedy, this film also looks at larger political issues.  Dad Yehuda is a committed peace activist and furious at Netanyahu for inflaming the crisis for his political ends.  On a tour of the US, he upsets his family for ‘going off-script’ and arguing with people whose help they are seeking.  “If I can talk to that…  anti abortionist (US Senator Mitch) McConnel,” excoriates him Liat’s US-based sister, then he too could avoid unnecessary confrontations.  Yehuda’s younger brother, now living in the US, takes an even more radical position than Yehuda in support of an unconditional ceasefire.  Liat is eventually released.  She, too, is a committed peace activist.  Months later, on a school trip to Yad Vashem holocaust memorial she points an exhibit on Warsaw’s ghetto wall.  This enabled people living outside the ghetto to ignore was going on inside, she observes.  Later, to the camera, she compares that ghetto wall to the fence separating Gaza from Israel which facilitated her own and Israeli public and nonchalance at Palestinian suffering.  “There are 15 million people living between the Mediterranean and the Jordan river,” contends Yehuda, “roughly half are Jews and the other half Palestinians.  We need to find a way of living together without killing each other.”  The filmmakers and the family members in attendance received a standing ovation at the packed Berlinale premiere.  Recommended.

title: GROWING DOWN
body: In this solid Hungarian debut feature, a widower attempts to cover up for his temperamental 12 year old son, whom he suspects responsible for a serious accident suffered by his new girlfriend’s daughter. While I question the aesthetic choice of shooting in very drab monochrome, it is well paced and features a superb performance by the 12 year old boy. Recommended.

title: ISLANDS
body: Tom is a washed out alcoholic English tennis  coach in Fuerteventura resort who gets embroiled with a visiting British family.  when the husband disappears, he and the wife become suspects.  An entertaining though ultimately unsatisfying mystery that fizzles out towards the end.  I would say this do for enjoyable but forgettable viewing on a streaming platform, not really film festival material.

title: HOME SWEET HOME
body:
Single mother Sofie starts working as a home carer for elderly people.  She is warm, conscientious and is well liked by her clients.   However in time she begins to struggle following an unjustified complaint about her ‘attitude‘ by a relative of one of the clients.  “My taxes pay her salary!” Another client, probably demented, is aggressive. She is frustrated by her boss’s health and safety rules that compromise the level of service she would like to offer.  An underperforming colleague upsets her. A client she is close to inevitably dies.  Her young daughter begins to feel neglected and their relationship suffers…. Thankfully it all works out in the end.  
Despite the somewhat predictable narrative, this is truely a superbly cast and observed drama.  I have never seen such graphic depiction of that kind of care work:  from cleaning of clients who have soiled themselves to the replacement of stoma bags.  It feels very real yet essential for our appreciation of what Sofie is facing.  Highly recommended.

title: SANDBAG DAM
body:
High school student’s Marko’s life in a small Croatian village is upended by the return of his friend Slaven from Berlin for his father’s funeral. Three years before, Slaven was kicked out of home after Marko’s mother caught them in flagrante delicto.  
In this, her second film, Čeren Černik Čanak wisely chose the more interesting perspective of Marko rather than Slaven which was the focus of the original script. The villagers are busy creating sandbag dams to protect the village from a flooding river: an elegant metaphor for the suppression of Marko and Slaven’s love. Not a single frame is wasted in this beautifully cast and observed film. Very highly recommended.

title: NIGHT STAGE
body: Queer noir with sexy hot men in a sweltering, dangerous city (Porto Alegre, Brazil.) Mattias, an ambitious young actor hooks up with Rafael, an older closeted politician. They discover they share a dangerous fetish for public sex.  Shot mostly at night with a richly saturated palette, this transgressive and at times explicit film is sure to please some audiences. I liked it. Recommended.

title: ALL I HAD WAS NOTHINGNESS
original_title: JE N’AVAIS QUE LE NÉANT - “SHOAH” PAR LANZMANN
body: Claude Lanzmann’s 9.5hr doc, SHOAH, was released in 1985, 12 years in the making.  Lanzmann interviewed victims, perpetrators and also these who lived close to the killing fields.  The result is considered by many as one of the most important documentaries ever made on any subject.  Lanzmann left over 220 hours of footage that was not used in his documentary and filmmaker Guillome Ribot uses these, with voiceover readings of Lanzmann’s memoirs and writings to reveal the process of the making of the documentary:  the fruitless search for funding in America, the subterfuge needed to get interviews with perpetrators, his long search for survivors and the process of working with them.  Fascinating for anyone interested in documentary fimmmaking and not just the holocaust.

title: MOTHER’S BABY
body: Successful orchestra conductor Julia and her husband go to a private fertility clinic where the creepily charismatic Dr Vilafort offers to them help with his experimental procedure. Julia becomes pregnant but at childbirth - masterfully captured in a single long take - her baby is taken away due to complications with the umbilical cord.  The baby is returned to the couple a few days later but Julia suspects something is wrong…. Is is postpartum depression or is it something else?  Great performance from Marie Leuenberger as Julia.  Minor irritation for me:  all outdoor shots appear to have been shot at the same time even though some must logically have taken place during different seasons.  Very watchable. . <This message was edited>

title: BEDROCK
body: The holocaust in Poland took place on hundreds of sites, most of which have no visible reminders of their past.  Kinga Michalska visited some of these places with her crew and captured scenes with local residents.  A Polish Jew visits a construction site of a new highway in a forest and urges workers to alert him if they come across any bones.  Two generations of a family argue about Polish complicity in the Jedwabne progrom that took place nearby.  A resident tells that her home is in the former camp where Josef Mengle carried out his grisly experiments on pregnant women.  Other locals complain about inconsiderate tourists in Birkenau.  Towards the end of the documentary Michalska tries to inject contemporary relevance by visiting the Belarusian-Polish border where many recent refugees have been killed or disappeared. A very slow contemplative film.

title: OLMO
body: Sweet coming of age film about a 14 year old Mexican-American boy in 1979 New Mexico, who would rather go to a party with beautiful Nina than stay at home to look after his MS-addled father. <This message was edited>

title: KONTINENTAL 25
body: The story of a bailiff distressed over the suicide of a homeless man she evicted sounded promising but was ultimately another disappointing competition entry. Although not legally responsible, she is hounded on social media by Romanian nationalists (she is ethnic Hungarian) and feels morally responsible.  After dispatching her husband and children on holiday to Greece, she seeks solace in four lengthy and unconvincing encounters with a colleague, her mother, a former student and her priest. Any redeeming quality:  the outdoor shots in the beautiful Transylvanian city of Cluj. Not recommended.

title: LURKER
body: Matthew lives with his grandmother in Los Angeles when Oliver, a rising musical artist comes into the clothing store where he works. In short order Matthew is invited to hang out with Oliver and his crew. Alex Russell expertly observes the dynamics of their relationship and the competition among the entourage for Oliver’s attention and affection. When Oliver tires of Matthew’s antics and abandons him in London, Matthew manages to blackmail his way back in to Oliver’s life.  A gripping and superbly cast study about obsessive fandom.  Highly recommended.

title: LATE SHIFT
body:
Leonie Benesch who delivered a fantastic performance in the Ilker Çatak’s THE TEACHERS’ LOUNGE stars in this superior hospital drama.  Director Petra Volpe’s camera follows her during a single shift at a Swiss hospital as the pressures mount and mistakes are inevitably made.  
Hospitals are fertile grounds for TV and movie dramas.  The popularity of TV shows like ER and Amazon Prime’s new series, THE PITT, are a testament to that.  What distinguishes this film is Volpe’s tight narrative focus on this particular character and Benesch’s sensitive performance. Recommended.

title: KÖLN 75
body: I am not a jazz fan. I don’t think I have even heard before any of Keith Jarrett’s music.  Yet I absolutely loved this terrific feel-good movie about the true story of an 18 year old promoter who booked Keith Jarrett’s 1975 concert at the Cologne Opera House.  A freelance journalist who follows Jarrett on his tour, provides occasional funny but informative contextual explanations about how Jarrett’s music sits in the history of Jazz.  I know this sounds awkward, but it really works.  Highly recommended. <This message was edited>

title: YUNAN
body: A depressed writer of Middle Eastern origin leaves Hamburg for a remote island where he intends to commit suicide. There he meets an innkeeper (Hannah Schygulla), with whom he gradually develops a bond.  This  is a very slow burning and enigmatic film which invites the audience to read their own meaning into what they see.

title: THE GOOD SISTER
body:
After being kicked out by her girlfriend, Rose moves in with her brother Sam, whom she adores.  A few nights later, sleeping on the living room sofa, Rose is disturbed by some noises from her brother’s bedroom. She gets up for a drink of water and sees a woman who emerges from her brother’s room and staring briefly at her, wordlessly leaves the apartment.  Some days later Rose receives a summons from the police to testify about what she witnessed that night.  At the police station Rose denies seeing anything but is then read the victim’s statement about having been raped by Sam.  Later in the apartment Rose finds some exculpatory evidence that supports that woman’s version.  when charges against the brother are dismissed due to lack of evidence, Rose is left with a grave moral dilemma. 
Tightly told, convincing and well acted family drama, replete elegant metaphorical references.  Recommended.

title: THE MESSAGE
body:
Young Anika possesses a gift:  she can channel the feelings and thoughts of animals.  Her grandparents monetize that gift by traveling with Anika through Argentina in their funky camper van to offer her services to pet owners.  (For these clients they cannot physically reach, the service is offered ‘online’ as Anika can also apparently connect with animals through emailed photos.)  Indeed, as the grandmother explains to perspective clients, a vet can cure physical ills but only Anika can mend the souls of their pets.  A brief stop is made at a psychiatric hospital where Anika is allowed a brief visit with her mum.  Much later, in the film’s pivotal and utterly unconvincing scene, Anika tells her grandmother that a bird told her that Anika’s mum loves the grandmother, eliciting a rare emotional response from her crusty guardian.
A VARIETY reviewer reminded me of the similarity between this film and Peter Bogdanovich 1973 PAPER MOON.  Both were shot in black and white with depressed modern day Argentina standing in for depression era USA.  It’s been a long time since I have seen it but regretfully I can confirm that EL MENSAJE lacks the original’s humour and pathos.  (Not everyone agrees, this film won the Silver Bear jury prize at the Berlinale.) <This message was edited>

title: L INTERET D ADAM
body:
L’Interet d’Adam
https://www.semainedelacritique.com/en/edition/2025/movie/l-interet-d-adam
4.5/5
This opening film of the Semaine de la Critique (which runs alongside the ‘official’ Cannes Film Festival) is highly influenced by Dardenne brothers social drama style and did not disappoint.  Lucy, a nurse in a public hospital’s pediatric section, is caring for 3 year old Adam. A court deemed his fracture is due to malnutrition caused by the mother’s unconventional dietary ideas and has restricted her access.  Yet the boy will not eat without his mum.  The film follows the nurse as she tries to act in the boy’s best interest. Director Laura Wandel rightly refuses to offer a pat and simple solution in this, her second feature. A strong script, her tight direction and superb performances deliver a powerful dramatic punch without resorting to any crass sentimentalism.

title: SOUND OF FALLING
body: The opening salvo of the ‘Competition’ section is this portrait of four generations of women living on a farm in Germany.  There is a mixture of filmic styles at play here with the oldest generation captured with languid, studied, almost frozen compositions.  I found it all unbearably dull and left after 80m.  (I did not think it is fair to rate it based on what I saw.)

title: ENZO
body: Sixteen year old Enzo is a boy on the cusp of manhood.  To the chagrin of his upper middle class parents who would have preferred him to continue his studies, he has decided to train as a apprentice mason.  At work he develops a romantic interest in his master, the hunky Ukrainian laborer Vlad who is almost twice his age.  Viewers seeking titillation will be disappointed.  Instead, Cantanet delivers a classical, unhurried and sensitively observed coming of age drama about Enzo’s grappling with inchoate yearnings he doesn’t fully comprehend and his parents’ and Vlad’s ambivalence on how to confront them

title: TWO PROSECUTORS
body:
During Stalin’s reign of terror in the 1930s, a freshly appointed provincial prosecutor receives a smuggled petition from a prisoner who claims to have been tortured to extract a false confession  that would incriminate himself and others. The prosecutor decides to pursue an investigation and to reach out to the chief state prosecutor in Moscow for help.  This solid Ukrainian entry to the ‘Competition’ section deftly exposes how decent, courageous individuals are caught up in tyrannies.  Recommended.  
4/5. <This message was edited>

title: A PALE VIEW OF THE HILLS
body:
A visually ravishing and haunting Japanese postwar drama that will reward a second viewing.
Before he wrote REMAINS IF THE DAY, the book that made him famous, British-Japanese writer Kazuo Ishiguro wrote two first person novels where the characters relate their postwar experiences.  In both novels (this film is based on his first) it becomes evident that what the characters relate about their past is not quite as they pretend.  While this works well in the novels, it is a little trickier in a film where a viewer might be perplexed by the alternate reality shown. Then again, film festivals are made for more demanding films.  Recommended

title: LA MISTERIOSA MIRADA DEL FLAMENCO
body:
1982, Atacama desert in north Chile.  Eleven year old Lidia lives with her trans sex worker mother Flamenco in a bordello catering to the local mining community.  AIDS is ravaging Flamenco and her colleagues and now that the miners too are getting sick, they are becoming scared and angry.  Yovani, Flanenco’s client/lover brutally kills her. Soon his colleagues decide to hold siege to the bordello.  But things do not proceed as expected.  Not at all!
It takes great talent to inject as much humor, pathos, courage, empathy and generousity of spirit as this film has given its tragic subject matter. Very strongly recommended

title: SIRAT
body:
During a recent visit to Ko Phangan, a Thai island famous for its full moon raves, I kept running into posters, left by relatives, seeking information on partygoers who disappeared. Luis is one such parent. Together with his younger son he is looking for his daughter from whom they have not heard for five months. Some people they encounter in a rave in Morocco do not recognize his daughter, but suggest she may be headed to another party taking place in the south of the country, near the Mauritanian border.  
Suddenly the army shows up and interrupts the party. A state of emergency has been declared and the foreigners are ordered to get into their vehicles and head home.  A few of the hard-core partygoers, decide to break off from the convoy. Luis, thinking that they may lead him to this second rave, decides to follow them.
Thus begins a mesmerizing road trip through the Moroccan desert.  The partygoers into whose company Luis and his son are reluctantly accepted are an odd bunch.  We learn little about their backstories from what they tell us.  Much more is expressed by their (not tender) age and rough physical aspect.  Very good cinema here. I was kept on the edge of my seat by the sometimes shocking turns, yet often invited to reflect on what was left unsaid.  Highly recommended

title: AMRUM
body: A beautifully shot and sensitively observed coming of age film. The war is ending and on Amrum island, off the northern coast of Germany, 12 year old Manning is helping support his mother, aunt and siblings. The nominal premise of the film seems banal, if not offensive: Manning’s  mother, depressed over the death of the Führer, refuses to eat anything other than white bread, butter and honey. The lengths to which Manning goes to try to placate her is the main narrative drive.  Yet it all works.  Magic.  Very highly recommended

title: THE LITTLE SISTER
body: A well directed and cast French coming out drama.  This time, the protagonist is 19-year old Fatima, a devout Muslim growing up in France.  After being accused of being a lesbian by a gay classmate who is bullied by her friends, Fatima dumps her very dumpable boyfriend and meets women on a dating app.  Eventually she hooks up with a Korean nurse. Their brief torrid affair is ended when the nurse lapses into one of her manic depressive episodes. Fatima turns to the local imam for advice. Not a good idea… After some more tribulations Fatima finds a way forward.  Not an earth shattering film, but good for the genre and very watchable

title: DOSSIER 137
body:
This solid competition entry follows police internal affairs investigation of police brutality against a yellow vest demonstrator during the riots that shook Paris in 2018.  
Lèa Drucker, who also appeared in L’INTERET D’ADAM, also in this Festival, here too gives a nuanced and convincing performance.  This genre film about institutional miscarriage of justice is particularly well directed and edited. I was struck by some powerful montage sequences:  the initial correspondence with the bureaucracy to collect evidence, the search for cctv footage and the police interrogations of suspects.  Highly recommended

title: DRUNKEN NOODLES
body: Gay male audiences who were deprived of titillation in ENZO, another queer title in this festival, will find plenty in this film about a graduate student’s summer in New York. Titillation, but not much else

title: NEW WAVE
body: May 1959. Jean Luc Godard feels restless in Paris. He steals some cash from the offices of CAHIERS DU CINEMA where he works and drives down to Cannes to attend the premiere of his friend Truffaunt’s 400 BLOWS. There he convinces a producer friend to back his first feature: BREATHLESS.  One can’t think of a more appropriate film to see at a Cannes film festival than this affectionate homage to French new wave cinema.  Besides the principals in that film, almost everyone is there: Chabrol, Melville, Rivette Resnais…. The attention to style and detail is fantastic, from the choice of font in the titles, down to the projectionist cues and end-of-reel scratches. Remember them?   But this is not just a tedious style piece.  Instead Linklater exposes Godard’s revolutionary techniques:  from single take shooting, the improvised script (or more precisely the absence of one), choice of hand held camera and fast Ilford film stock (to avoid the need for artificial lighting in interiors), use of passers by as unwitting extras on scenes shot in the streets of Paris, the choppy editing to keep the audience uncomfortable. Brilliant. Highly recommended
