title: NINO
body:
On Friday 29 year old Nino receives a cancer diagnosis. He is told treatment will start on Monday.  This film follows him over the weekend spent with his mother, ex-girlfriend, a friend who organizes a surprise birthday party and an ex-schoolmate he meets by chance.
It is a good premise let down by a lucklustre script.despite a strong performance by Theodore Pellerin

title: ORWELL 2+2=5
body: Essay and novel excerpts, diary entries and letters by George Orwell are the only words spoken in this masterfully edited documentary illustrated with historical and contemporary footage, stills and clips from various renditions of 1984 and ANIMAL FARM amongst others.  All these illustrate how prescient Orwell was about our present

title: MAMA
body:
Mila is a migrant live-in housekeeper for a wealthy Israeli couple. On an unplanned return back to Ukraine, she discovers that her husband has taken on a lover and her daughter wants to ditch her university studies to marry the boyfriend that impregnated her. She concocts a plan to have an ultrasound examination of the pregnancy falsely recommend an abortion.  A just about watchable film. However, I have seen these themes treated better in other films. 
2/5 <This message was edited>

title: THE SECRET AGENT
body:
A dead body lies rotting for days in a petrol station forecourt.  He has been shot by the station attendant when trying to steal some motor oil. When the police eventually show up, they are more interested on fleecing a passing motorist than attending to the crime.  Brazil, 1977, a time of great mischief, where corruption rules and most human life is worthless. 
The main plot concerns a university professor trying to evade a hit ordered against him by a corrupt government-connected businessman.  While the fantastic production design is very evocative of the period, Memdonçha Filho crams too many distracting tangents. (One quite funny, involves an out of control severed leg.) Despite the overlong running time, the ending feels abrupt and anticlimactic (to borrow the word from my friend Nando.)
3/5 <This message was edited>

title: EAGLES OF THE REPUBLIC
body: Director Saleh and his lead Fares reprise their collaboration (THE NILE HILTON AFFAIR) in this brooding and atmospheric political thriller. Here Fares switches roles. Instead of being the manipulative and chilling secret police operative he plays a star of Egyptian cinema being compelled to make a propaganda film for the regime.  Saleh pulls no punches in this portrayal of the Al-Sisi regime, which was shot in Turkey.  Fares gives a nuanced performance as an artist who tries to navigate in very treacherous currents.  Recommended

title: PILLION
body: Meek and timid parking inspector Colin falls for a handsome biker who appreciates his “aptitude for devotion.”  This explicit and not so tender master-slave love story is hightened by touches of humor and superb performances by Melling and Skarsgārd

title: ALPHA
body:
The considerable talents and efforts of Tahar Rahim (LE PROPHET, THE MAURITANIAN) and Melissa Boros are wasted in this histrionic AIDS allegory.  The plague here ossifies its victims into marble like statues that cough dust but the setting of an early nineties France is retained.  Director Docornau appears more interested in the body horror aesthetics than any real depth or plausibility.  Rahim must have gone on a killer diet for this role of an infected addict. A pity.
2/5 <This message was edited>

title: ELEANOR THE GREAT
body:
Best friends Bessie and Eleanor have been happily living together in Florida after their husbands died years ago.  When Bessie passes, Eleanor moves in with her divorced daughter and grandson in Manhattan.  Feeling bored and lonely, Eleanor accidentally stumbles on an holocaust survivor support group meeting at the Jewish Community Center.  There she tells her story.  Except Eleanor grew up in America and did not experience the holocaust… 
Scarlett Johansson’s comedy drama is elevated by the witty and sassy role of Eleanor, ably performed by June Squibb.  It was a little too sentimental for my taste but it is sure to please many audiences

title: UN SIMPLE ACCIDENT
body:
Black comedy about former political inmates of who kidnap one of the men they think has tortured them.  (They are not entirely certain he is the right person.  While in prison they only heard his voice and the shuffle of his prosthetic leg.)  
This is one of these projects that sound promising as a concept pitched to producers but that is actually very tricky to make work.  Sorry, I don’t think Panahi quite succeeds

title: THE SIX BILLION DOLLAR MAN
body:
Julian Assange is no angel but he made a very important contribution to our knowledge of the truth, claims whistleblower Edward Snowden in an interview that opens Andrew Jarecki’s [CAPTURING THE FRIEDMANS, THE JINX] sympathetic documentary on the Wikileaks founder.  While this film does not quite shatter mythe perception that Assange is an arrogant and probably not entirely pleasant man, it did provide evidence for some serious claims that I was unaware of:
- Following the incident where Reuters journalists were shot, the company made enquiries with the US army which denied wrongdoing.  The release of the helicopter video of the killing by Wikileaks proved otherwise.
- Wikileaks released a great deal of evidence of mistreatment and killing of civilians in Iraq and Afghanistan by allied forces than had been previously acknowledged by them.
- There was a genuine effort by Wikileaks and its media partners to redact the release of the Embassy cables in order to prevent named individuals from being endangered.  This was undermined by the irresponsible action of a greedy GUARDIAN journalist.
- For three years after he became president, Obama failed to bring about the end of the Iraq war which he promised.  It was the release by Wikileaks of a particularly shocking US war crimes incident that lead to Prime Minister Maliki withdrawing immunity from US servicemen and Obama’s subsequent decision to end US engagement in Iraq.  In effect Wikileaks helped end the war.
- Instead of addressing the war crimes revealed by Wikileaks the US decided to conduct, with the help of allies, a campaign against Assange.  The women who demanded he be forced to undergo an HIV test, were pressured to sign rape complaints by the police.  
- During his stay at the Ecuadorian embassy, Assange was subject to surveilance by the Americans (unbeknownst to the Ecuadorians.)
- The indictment filed by the US government calling for his extradition from Britain rested on a highly unreliable witness.
Having read the above, is it still worth going to see this film?  I think so. 
4/5 <This message was edited>

title: THE DISAPPEARANCE OF JOSEF MENGELE
body: Most of us won’t need Serebrennikov’s dramatization to realize that Dr Josef Mengele, who conducted dubious experiments on inmates at Auschwitz, was probably not a very pleasant man.  Shot mostly in monochrome, the film charts Mengele’s postwar period: the time in Buenos Aires where he escaped after the war and had to flee following an accusation that he was involved in an illegal abortion, his brief visit to Germany after the war, his terror of being captured and killed by the Israelis (the fate of his colleague Eichmann) which led him to hide in a sordid Brazilian farm shielded by an unfriendly Hungarian family and later in an even more sordid home in the outskirts of Sao Paolo, where he died in 1979. The brief sequences that are not in monochrome are of the wartime period, giving us the dubious benefit of seeing one of the less gory ‘experiments’ in vivid colours.  Serebrennikov and his star August Diell appear to want to stick to what is known rather than speculate on any psychological motivations or displays of ‘remorse’. Thankfully, Mengele is not portrayed as a sociopath but rather as a nasty man who knew he had good reasons to be scared. If it’s any consolation, he appears to have led a very miserable life after the war. Even the visit of his son Rolf does not appear to bring him any joy. Yet I was left ambivalent on the value of this cinematic experience

title: SENTIMENTAL VALUE
body: In Joachim Trier’s family drama, an ageing art house film director (Stellan Skarsgārd), whose career is in decline, is seeking to make a film with his partly estranged elder daughter. (Renate Reinsve). There are multiple layers of trauma at play here.  The director’s mother killed herself when he was seven.  He was a largely absent father to his daughters.  There are some exquisitely observed moments here, carried by outstanding performances.  I only wish it had a tighter narrative focus

title: ROMERÍA
body:
I wish I had seen Carla Simón’s previous two films, which like this one, appear to draw from her own life experience.  Simon was orphaned at a very young age:  her parents IV drug users who succumbed to AIDS.  In this film 19-year old Marina (the beautiful and confident Llucia Garcia), comes to Vigo to secure partenity documents she needs to secure a scholarship to film school.  She soon discovers that her wealthy grandparents have falsified her father’s death certificate because they were ashamed of their son’s diagnosis and held his wife (who appears to share an uncanny resemblance to Marina) for his addiction.  
Recommended

title: LOVE ME TENDER
body:
Amicably separated Camille shares custody of 11 year old Paul with her husband Laurent. One day, over coffee, she tells him that she has started dating women. Laurent seems to take it in stride and says that he wants her to be happy. Nevertheless, when Camille stops a few days later to pick Paul, the boy tells his mother he hates her and refuses to come with her.  He also refuses to talk to her when she calls.  Some weeks later she gets notice that Laurent is suing for full custody.  
This film follows Camille’s struggle to reclaim her maternal rights in the face of her determined and angry husband.  Yes, it is a story that has been told before, but here it is told particularly well with good character development and a surprising outcome. My only regret is that it could have been edited a little more tightly with some unnecessary tangents dispensed with.  Recommended

title: THE HISTORY OF SOUND
body:
Lionel (Paul Mescal), from a humble background but with a keen musical ear ends up in the Boston conservatory of music where he meets fellow student David (Josh O’Connor).  Together they embark on a journey together through 1920s rural America recording folk songs and ballads.
This tender, slow burning gay love story may lack the explosive fiery passion of a BROKEBACK MOUNTAIN or GOD’S OWN COUNTRY but remains deeply affecting.  The wonderful Chris Cooper (longtime John Sayles collaborator), appears as the older David.  Highly recommended.
4.5/5 <This message was edited>

title: JEUNES MÈRES
body:
A shelter for young and expactant mothers is the setting for this latest offering from the Dardenne brothers focusing in on five of them. There is one who fantasizes that she can set up a home with her no good petty criminal boyfriend. Another, traumatized by being abandoned by her birth mother, stalks her and contemplates doing the same with her baby. A third, living with her alcoholic mother and the mother’s abusive boyfriend, wants to give the child away despite her own mother’s desire to keep it… You get the idea.
As a big fan of the Dardenne brothers whose LE FIL blew me away when I first saw it, I was left disappointed by this effort which felt almost like a condensed social realist soap opera.  Indeed, I think some of the Dardenne’s artistic disciples are now making better films:  Laura Wandel’s L’INTERET D’ADAM (in this festival) and Petra Volpe’s HELDIN (premieredin Berlin this year.)

title: LA GRAZIA
body:
Sorrentino’s new film was chosen for the opening of the festival. (The gala presentation is this evening, but I attended the morning press screening.) I was reluctant to go as I found PARTHENOPE, his previous film at last year’s festival, silly,  boring and altogether unwatchable.  But this one was, dare I say, very good.
Longtime Sorrentino star Toni Servillo plays the president of Italy, a widower, who as he approaches retirement ponders whether to sign an euthanasia bill and approve two clemency petitions for convicted murderers. (‘Grazia’ means both clemency and grace in Italian.) All the while, grieving departed wife, he is tormented by an affair she had 40 years before with, he suspects, his best friend.  Although Sorrentino cannot help including some of his trademark tangential sentimental cinematic flourishes, substance trumps style and all is delivered with an appropriate dose of humour

title: BUGONIA
body:
Long time Lanthimos collaborator Jesse Plemmons brilliantly plays a beekeeper who is convinced that aliens are trying to eradicate humanity. Together with his simple-minded cousin, he concocts a plot to kidnap a top corporate executive (an amazing Emma Stone) whom he believes is one of these aliens.
I was never a Lanthimos fan.  After last year’s KINDS OF KINDNESS, which I intensely disliked, I was not expecting much. However he, like Sorrentino (with LA GRAZIA), pleasantly surprised me. Topical and clever in its exploration of conspiracy theories and oncoming dystopian catastrophes, this blackest of black comedies is deliciously dark and funny.  
4/5 <This message was edited>

title: JAY KELLY
body:
If there was a Cary Grant or a Gary Cooper for our age then it would surely be George Clooney. In Noah Baumbach’s new film for Netflix he plays an actor very much styled on himself that is trying to reconnect with his two daughters that feel he has abandoned them for the sake of his career.  
A little overlong and a bit heavy on sentimentality this in not quite at the level of Baumbach‘s previous effort for Netflix, WHITE NOISE.  Nevertheless it is worth streaming, if only for the very tender scene about 120 minutes in, between Clooney and Adam Sandler

title: GHOST ELEPHANTS
body:
Https://www.labiennale.org/en/cinema/2025/out-competition/ghost-elephants
What would compel a veteran director like Werner Herzog to direct, write and narrate a nature documentary for National Geographic?  It is his interest in men driven by epic obsessions.  
For ten years Dr Steve Boyes nursed an epic obsession to find an elusive breed of what he terms ‘ghost elephants’ so called because hardly any human has seen them, who are said to inhabit one of the most remote parts of the planet: a wetlands area in a high plateau the size of the UK in eastern Angola. These are said to be the largest elephants in Africa, hence the largest living mammals on earth. This is what compels Boyes, much like the character Klaus Kinski played in Herzog’s FITZCARRALDO in his quest to build an opera house in the Amazon, to recruit San Bushmen animal trackers from northern Namibia on an epic expedition, hundreds of miles into these impenetrable highlands, using motorbikes hand lifted by his crew over rivers, in his quest to find them.  Herzog brings us along for the adventure.  At this  year’s festival, Francis Ford Coppola presented Herzog the golden lion. 
4/5 <This message was edited>

title: ORPHAN
body:
Laszlo Nemes’s 2015 SON OF SAUL, about inmates forced to work in the gas chambers of Auschwitz, was one of the grimmest films ever made.  His latest film is about survivors. 
Five years after the war, Andover Hirsch is plucked out of an orphanage by his mother, who was hidden during the war by a gentile butcher.  In 1957, shortly after the failed Hungarian uprising which Andover sympathized with but was unable to participate in due to his youth, he is still waiting for his father to show up.  While he seeks to learn about his father and his faith from his old colleagues, his father’s synagogue and his best friend’s more observant family, the butcher shows up. Nemes’s powerful and unflinching portrayal of Jewish life in postwar Hungary is deeply sobering and sheds a spotlight on deep traumas suffered even by these who managed to evade the camps

title: À PIED D’ŒUVRE WORK
body:
Back in 2001, the American writer Barbara Ehrenreich published NICKLED AND DIMED a sobering but at times very humorous book about the indignities faced by middle aged unskilled workers (such as the newly single former ‘homemaker’ she pretends to be) forced into low income work.  Ehrenreich’s book was written before the advent of the gig economy but it’s theme is very reminiscent of Donzelli’s small but worthy competition entry.
Paul has ditched his successful photography career to devote himself to writing. His previous two books have met critical but not financial success and his publisher is wary of publishing his latest depressing novel inspired by the breakup of his marriage.  Short of funds, Paul moves into a small studio owned by his sister and begins his journey into the gig economy as a handyman and a ride-share driver.  The book he eventually emerges with, and much of this movie, is a contemporary adaptation of Erenreich’s work.  One scene that struck me was when a passenger, an acquaintance from Paul’s time as a photographer, recognizes him and wonders what he is doing driving cars. After providing a few curt answers, Paul turns on the car radio for the rest of the trip.  Recommended.
4/5 <This message was edited>

title: COVER
body:
Without Seymour Hersh we would have probably not learned of the My Lai massacre, much about the CIA complicity in Pinochet’s coup in Chile, the tortures at Abu Ghraib and countless other abuses before, between and since.  Hersh always wanted to expose the policy and these truly responsible rather than accept the convenient ‘fall guys’ that are usually sacrificed (such as William Calley, the only person actually prosecuted for My Lai.)
Hersh comes accross an intensely private and in his own words, distrustful person.  It took Laura Poitras (CITIZEN K) and Obenhaus over 20 years to convince him to participate in this documentary about his life and work.  He recently published an excellent autobiography, REPORTER. But we learn even more about him and his methods from this film.  His interviews with Poitras are constantly interrupted by phone calls from sources and contacts, while Poitras’s camera keeps rolling.  Poitras interviews some of his living sources while Hersh reveals some backstories about some (dead) others.  We glimpse his very cryptic notes and densely annotated Rolodex.  There are some awkward moments when Poitras clearly draws him out of his comfort zone and the film does confront his errors.  This is a superb documentary about one of the greatest practitioners of a vital but highly maligned profession.
5/5 <This message was edited>

title: MY FATHER AND QADDAFI
body: Jihan was only 6 years old when her father, Mansur Kikhia disappeared after being abducted out of his hotel  in Cairo.  He was a former Libyan diplomat who had defected to the opposition, so the culprit was quite obvious.  For years, Jihan, her mother and siblings hoped in vain for his return. In this sometimes moving, but overlong personal documentary, Jihan explores what happened to her father, family and country

title: AFTER HUNT
body:
Undoubtedly the hottest ticket in Venice this year is Guadagnino’s me-too film, AFTER THE HUNT. It’s a bit of a damp squib.
Julia Roberts plays a Yale professor who is told by one of her students that Robert’s colleague and best friend has raped her.  To spice this tired narrative the student is a black lesbian, in a relationship with a gender fluid individual, with very rich parents who are major contributors to Yale, had been caught by the man she accused of having plagiarized  on her dissertation and probably in love with Roberts. Ah, yes, and the accused and Roberts have had an affair and the girl has found secret evidence of that prior to making her accusation.  All a bit tiresome if you ask me.  But go if you want to see a very elegant Roberts gliding through some beautifully decorated interiors

title: LOUIS MALLE LE RÉVOLTÉ
body: Louis Malle’s adoption of very distinct styles for each of his films is the reason critics have often rated him less than less accomplished contemporaries.  At 24 he abandoned his studies to intern with Cocteau who co-credited him as director on an underwater documentary. For ASCENSOUR POR L’ECHAFAND he plucked Miles Davis out of a Paris nightclub to improvise over a few days the haunting soundtrack.  Rich with wonderful clips and interviews, this excellent documentary made me want to revisit many of his works

title: FRANKENSTEIN
body: Guillermo del Toro’s adaptation of Shelley’s FRANKENSTEIN for Netflix is beautifully filmed, stunningly costumed and features superb production design.  It is also very entertaining. Worthy of going to the cinema for

title: MOTOR CITY
body: An ultra violent action thriller about a 1970s Detroit car factory worker out for revenge against the mobster who ‘stole’ his girl and the corrupt policeman that framed him is not something that I would usually go for.  But in terms of pure cinema, Ponciroli’s small independent feature is probably one of the best films in Venice this year.  Eschewing virtually any dialogue in favor of great soundtrack of 70s hits, this beautifully filmed and production designed film feels like a contemporary dance theatre ballet (think Matthew Bourne or Pina Bausch.) I was left with my jaw dropped for almost 103 minutes. Very highly recommended!

title: IL MAESTRO
body: At times charming but sadly entirely forgettable coming of age competition entry about a young teenage tennis player and his psychologically damaged ex-pro coach

title: LE MAGE DU KREMLIN WIZARD KREMLIN
body: Oliver Assayas returns to Venice with this political thriller about a spin doctor who helps Putin’s rise to power.  While the character of Vadim Baranov is fictional, most of the characters and events are easily recognisable.  (Only Mikhail Khordorovsky, has his name changed in this film, presumably because he is still alive.)  At times actual news footage is melded into the film, such as the grieving relatives of Kursk mariners, the performing Pussy Riot protesters and some public appearances of Putin himself.  I would have not thought of casting Jude Law as Putin, but he seems to capture that sinister man’s character pretty well.  I am a little more troubled by baby-faced Paul Dano as Baranov.  The real life spin doctors that I am familiar with tend to be somewhat more profane, colourful and magnetic.  The character Dano plays comes across as fairly flat.  This film was described in a number of places are as a satire or comedy.   While I may have chuckled once at an ironical comment, it was mostly pretty sombre and riveting stuff

title: SOUFFLEUR
body:
William Defoe is an actor who seemingly can’t say ‘no’ to any script he is offered. You have to respect his dedication.  But I just couldn’t sit through to the end of this dull film about the manager of the Intercontinental Vienna.
1/5 <This message was edited>

title: SMASHING MACHINE
body:
Mark Kerr was one of the first professional practitioners of mixed martial arts MMA, an extremely violent and bloody form of spectator sport.  His terrifying power earned him the nickname ‘the smashing machine.’ Dwayne Johnson gives a powerful and nuanced performance in this solid competition entry. While the usual genre tropes are there: toxic relationship, addiction to painkillers, etc, this film is devoid of cheap sentimentality (a la ROCKY). Even more unexpected is the articulate and gentle nature of this hulk of a man.  In a brief coda with the real Kerr, it is evident Johnson was faithful to his character.
4/5 <This message was edited>

title: FATHER MOTHER SISTER BROTHER
body: Three separate shorts only very loosely thematically connected.  In the first, an adult brother (Adam Driver) and sister make a brief visit to the remote US lakeside home of a father (Tom Waits) they rarely see and who has been feigning penury in order to scam them.  In the second, two sisters visit their mother (Charlotte Rampling) who they see once a year for tea even though all three live in Dublin.  In the third, an American brother and a sister visit the empty Paris apartment of their parents, recently deceased in an air crash.  No plots as such, lots of awkward silences and the realization that these family members don’t really know much about one another.  Each short opens with a brief slo-mo surreal sequence of a few skateboarders passing our characters.  You either love Jim Jarmusch or you don’t

title: HOLOFICTION
body:
The six or so hours of Claude Lanzman’s SHOAH featured no archival footage and relied entirely on survivor testimony.  Indeed, he argued that any visual representations of such historical traumas, much more so FICTIONAL representations such as Spielberg’s SCINDLER’S LIST- were not only inadequate in conveying the horror but could be regarded transgressive or even obscene.  
From Chaplin’s 1940 THE GREAT DICTATOR to Glazer’s 2023 THE ZONE OF INTEREST, there have been hundreds of films that attempted to fictionalise the holocaust.  Assembling by my calculation over 3000 clips, most a mere 1-2 seconds long, with barely enough time to read the film’s name in the discretely displayed subtitle outside the frame, stripped of their sound and set to Paul Marzocchi’s original soundtrack, Michal Kosakovski created a masterful retelling of the holocaust narratives featuring all the visual tropes of the genre.
Brilliantly and fluidly edited (down to continuing tracking shots through different films), you have all the typical tropes repeated over and over:  from the introductory banal scenes such as putting on a record at home, ‘Jude’ being slapped on storefronts, people hiding and being discovered, victims turning back to gaze as they are being marched away, victims loaded onto trains, entering through the ‘Arbeit macho frei’ gates, smirking Nazis, and even the mood shots of the night moon.   There are several juxtapositions of the same actor playing opposite roles in different films: a Nazi Willem Defoe staring down a cowering victim Willem Defoe. A crazed Italian Fascist Donald Southerland smirking as a Jewish Donald Southerland drinks poison. There are the Nazi/Jewish Ben Kingsley, the Nazi/Jewish Harvey Keitel, the Nazi/Jewish Ralph Fiennes and many others I recognized but could not name. It left me mesmerized and yes, cognizant of how holofiction can reduce historical trauma to kitch

title: DEAD MAN’S WIRE
body:
Gus Van Sant returns with a dramatization of a criminal incident in that occurred in 1977, in Indianapolis.  Tony Kiritsis, in default on a commercial property loan which he felt was not extended because the mortgage company’s desire to defraud him of the property, walked into the president’s office. He wired a shotgun pointing to Richard Hall’s head in such a way that if Hall tried to escape or if Kiritsis was shot by a sniper, the shotgun would go off. Using this contraption, they proceeded to Kiritsis’s apartment. For 69 hours they sat there, making occasional calls into a local radio station until Kiritsis’s demands were accepted: immunity, a forgiveness of the loan, an apology and $5m ‘in compensation.’ As soon as the terms were agreed to and Hall released, Kirtisis was overpowered and prosecuted. To cheers of these present in the courtroom (and with me in the cinema) Kiritsis was found ‘not guilty by reason of insanity.’  Audiences also cheered when an end title revealed that the mortgage company went into administration a few years later.
To his credit, Van Sant maintains a neutral tone.  Attempts at humor are half hearted. This is no SUGARLAND EXPRESS. Kirtisis’s claims that he has been cheated are left as just that, the uncorroborated claims that he makes.  In a brief cameo as Hall’s father and the company’s chief executive, Al Pacino does come across as an heartless arsehole but Hall himself retains the film’s empathy. A brief coda shows him to have been deeply scarred by his trauma. Recommended

title: L’ÉTRANGER STRANGER
body: François Ozon’s classic interpretation, shot in loscious monochrome, appears very faithful to the plot and tone of Camus’s novel.  Ozon being Ozon, I guess he could not resist letting his camera linger on Benjamin Voisin’s attractive backside. I didn’t mind. Recommended

title: HOUSE DYNAMITE
body:
Titles at the beginning of Kathryn Bigelow new Netflix drama somberly inform us that after the Cold War, the great powers sought to reduce their nuclear arsenals but that now the situation has changed.  Her film imagines the 25 minutes when a ultra ballistic missile from an indeterminate source is seen crossing the Pacific towards the United States.  Confusingly many scenes are repeated as they are presented from multiple perspectives.  (That explains why it takes almost two hours to relate what  happens in 25 minutes.)  Not helping (despite the presence of subtitles in this screening) are the confusing quick-fire jargon and the use of multiple acronyms common to films about the US national security apparatus.  
Also, sadly, this film feels dated as it was conceived before Trump 2.0.   Happily the new President and his team would be much better skilled and morally equipped to deal with such crises

title: EN EL CAMINO
body:
Twenty year old Veneno is on the run.  He offers truck drivers lines of coke and his body.  Mexico’s roads are dangerous.  The truck drivers prefer to drive through the night without stopping and Veneno’s coke can keep them awake.  
At one rest stop Veneno convinces Muñeco to give him a ride.  Muñeco is not gay but not homophobic either.  David Pablo’s atmospheric noir deftly and convincingly portrays their burgeoning relationship and their tragic personal backstories.  Both Victor Prieto and Osvaldo Sanchez offer masterful performances.  Strong language, violence and explicit sex scenes.  Highly recommended

title: VOICE HIND RAJAB
body:
In January 2024 a call was received by the Palestine Red Crescent call centre in Ramallah.  A panicked woman in Gaza had claimed that she was in her car, in a military-restricted area, being shot at by an Israeli tank. Before the woman could give her name, gunfire was heard and the call was terminated.  Soon afterwards another call was received. The woman’s relative from Germany called to say that the woman was not alone in the car. Besides her husband and four daughters, all of whom had been killed, her 6 year old niece was still alive.  Although an ambulance was only 8 minutes away, it could not be sent to her without coordinating safe passage with the Israeli army.  For several hours the call centre staff tried to reassure the young girl that help was on the way while they tried to negotiate permits through multiple intermediaries: a process that typically takes several hours.  When that was finally obtained and an ambulance sent to her, it too was shot at by the army.  Six days later Hind was found dead. The two paramedics sent to rescue her had also perished.
When someone dies while on the call, staff ask relatives to send them pictures of the deceased.  Hind was evidently a very sweet girl, one of thousands of innocent Palestinian and Israelis who have been cruelly and needlessly killed in this war.  Ben Hania  cleverly weaves original call recordings and a social media video of a social worker trying to calm Hind, with the dramatized footage.  
One qualm I have with this film is the scene where Omar, the staff member primarily in touch with Hind, throws a tantrum when the coordinator refuses to send the ambulance without the army authorization.  Although I wasn’t in the room, I strongly suspect that this scene was fabricated in order to ‘explain’ to the audience how suicidal such an action would be.  Even by January last year, scores of first responders have been killed in action.  However much traumatised Omar is, I could not believe him to be so reckless. I wish Ben Hania would have found a better way to convey this information without undermining credibility. Notwithstanding, I strongly recommend this timely and important film

title: ELISA
body:
This is one of these films where the introductory ‘based on actual events’ title is meant to make you overcome the feelings of disbelief that would otherwise engulf you.  But at any rate, if you intend to kill your sibling, burn their body and then attempt to do the same with your mum remember it is best to do it in Switzerland.
Ten years after her conviction we find Elisa in what must be the world’s most luxurious correctional institution.  In this place inmates are lodged in pretty wooden cabins with their own fully equipped kitchens set amidst beautiful woodland, in which they appear able to  freely roam.  They can also attend onsite lectures delivered by distinguished professors.  Here she undergoes sessions with a criminologist that help her confront her responsibility for the actions that brought her here.  In competition, but you can give this one a pass.
2/5 <This message was edited>

title: AÚN ES DE NOCHE EN CARACAS IT WOULD BE NIGHT CARACAS
body: It’s 2017 in Caracas and the streets are on fire. Adelaida just buried her mother, and returns home to find the locks changed and their apartment expropriated by women aligned with the regime.  Thus begins a tense political thriller about the nightmare reality of Bolivarian Venezuela and the desperate measures needed to escape it. Highly recommended

title: HAND DANTE
body:
A Sicilian mobster comes into the posession of the original manuscript of Dante Alighieri’s THE DIVINE COMEDY.  He reaches out to a New York mobster who double crosses him by sending a Dante expert (Oscar Isaac) and a hit man (Gerard Butler) to steal them.  Schnabel weaves the contemporary scenes shot in monochrome, with 14th century colour scenes when Dante (Isaac, again), wrote his poem while struggling with the Pope (Butler, too) who banished him from Florence.  There are great cameos by Malkovich, Al Pacino, Scorsese and Franco Nero.  Like in his previous films, Schnabel appears fascinated by the intersection of art and capital.  And this one too is overlong and touched by a sense of self importance. It does, however, have several memorable darkly funny moments. 
3-

title: TWO PIANOS
body: Famous pianist Matthias (François Civil, alternating between being teary eyed, fainting or just blind drunk) returns to Lyon for a concert with his old teacher (Rampling, wonderful as always but completely wasted here), when he catches sight of a boy in a park that utterly resembles his six year old self.  Turns out the boy is the child of Claude, partner of his best friend Pierre, with whom he had a brief affair some years before.  A few minutes into the movie Pierre conveniently suffers a heart attack and dies.  This is a shame because he is the only credible character in this pretentious overcooked drama

title: NOMAD SHADOW
body: In Elma Inamishi’s worthy debut feature, immigrant Mariam is deported back to Moroccan occupied Western Sahara after losing her marketing job and supporting herself selling Ecstasy in Spanish clubs.  The film follows her as she is forced to reacclimate into the repressive traditional society and rekindles her friendship with her outsider friend with whom she originally emigrated to Spain.  This delicately observed and well acted feature is only slightly marred by a clunky metaphor coda

title: THREE GOODBYES
body: In Coixet’s new Italian language film, chef Antonio leaves high school sports teacher Marta after seven years together.  She then becomes gravely ill.  Despite the sombre theme this beautifully observed, wise and generous film is a love poem to life and Rome.  Alba Rohrwacher is superb as the woman who shows us what’s truly important and how to appreciate it. Very highly recommended

title: AND SONS
body: An ageing highly successful writer, who has neither left his home nor written a word in twenty years, summons his two estranged adult sons to deliver an important message. What initially promised to be a fairly routine family reconciliation drama—perhaps even one tinged with moments of levity—quickly revealed itself to be something else entirely. An unexpected twist opens the door for Pablo Trapero to venture into new and compelling dramatic territory. The ever-reliable Bill Nighy and Imelda Staunton lead a strong cast, supported by an excellent soundtrack. Very highly recommended

title: THE ROAD BETWEEN US THE ULTIMATE RESCUE
body:
Amir Tibon and his family were hiding in the safe room of their home when Hamas terrorists attacked their Kibbutz Nahal Oz. Amir reached out to his father Noam, a retired general in Tel Aviv. Without hesitation the two grandparents got into their jeep to mount a rescue.  This film relates the story of the hours that followed by tracking Noam and Gali as they recreated their journey combined with Hamas livestream captures, security camera footage and interviews with survivors. 
There have been a couple of remarkable October 7th docs released in the last year.  I am thinking specifically of HOLDING LIAT and A LETTER TO DAVID. Sadly this is not one of them.  At the screening, producer Mark Shelby admitted that the entire shoot took just a couple of days and it sadly feels like it.  Rushed.  The slapped-on sappy emotional score was particularly grating. Nevertheless it is a story that deserves to be heard. 
However much I am disappointed by the missed opportunity here, I am annoyed by the attempts to shut it down.  The film  presents what happened on the one day in October.  Crimes against humanity are crimes against humanity regardless of who commits them.  This film is not an apologia for the Israeli response to October 7th just as THE VOICE OF HIND RAJAB does not have to address the attitudes of the Gaza population to the Hamas attack that preceded the war.  Yet TIFF invited, then disinvited and then re-invited this film. Ultimately there was only one screening, a sold out performance in the 2,000 seat Roy Thompson Hall but with a noisy demonstration outside and very stringent security.  Israeli filmmakers, often besieged by the Netanyahu government against which they stand in fierce opposition, now increasingly face calls for their boycott by their international colleagues.  it’s a shame

title: BAD APPLES
body:
On a school visit to a cider factory, a solitary sneaker is seen swirling among the apples towards the pulping chutes, about to cause mayhem to the machinery.  “Where is Danny?” asks the teacher.  A boy standing alone on one of the platforms smirks at us contemptuously.  The camera pans down to reveal he is wearing only one shoe.  Danny is a bad apple.  Impossible for schoolteacher Maria (Saoirse Ronan, fantastic) to control.  The looming visit by the government school inspector forces her to take drastic action with unexpected outcomes not just for Danny and Maria but the whole community.  Jonathan Etzler’s excellent satirical thriller keeps audiences on edge, amused and thinking.  Highly recommended.
5/5 <This message was edited>

title: FRANZ
body: Agnieszka Holland’s new film relates the mostly adult life of Franz Kafka as he would perhaps have experienced and related it.  Interspersed are occasional scenes satirising the crass commercialisation of the Kafka phenomenon in present day Prague.  I did like some of Holland’s previous films (most notably CHARLATAN) but I found this one at times tedious

title: GLENROTHAN
body: Brian Cox and Alan Cummings are two brothers, from a Scottish distillery family, reuniting after many years’ estrangement in this schmaltzy comedy drama/Scottish tourist board promo.  I greatly admire both actors but this, Brian Cox’s directorial debut, suggests he should stick to acting

title: RENTAL FAMILY
body: Philip, played wonderfully by Brendan Fraser is a none-too-successful American actor living in Japan.  His biggest hit was as a superhero character in a toothpaste commercial, when he lands a job for Rental Family.  This is one of hundreds of Japanese firms that supply professional actors to interact in emotional support roles.  In his first gig, which almost ends in disaster, he is hired by a lesbian, about to move abroad to live with her partner, to ‘marry’ her in a traditional ceremony for the benefit of her parents.  Another client hires him to boost the spirits of her ageing former actor father by ‘interviewing’ him for a film journal.  Yet another single mother needs him to be her daughter’s absent ‘father’ as the girl prepares for her high school entrance exams.  Hikari deftly and sensitively navigates a rich emotional terrain as the Philip overcomes his own reticence over his assignments and is increasingly drawn into the lives of his subjects.  (Brian Cox can learn a great deal from Hikari on making great comedy-dramas that promote tourist destinations.)  This audience pleaser is very highly recommended

title: BETWEEN DREAMS AND HOPE
body:
Azad is an Iranian trans man who wishes to marry his girlfriend Nora.  The State Commission that will determine whether he can initiate gender affirming treatment insists that he obtain the notarized consent of his estranged father.  Reluctantly, Azad and Nora head to the countryside to find daddy.  Not a good idea!  After being almost killed by dad and older brother, Azad is rescued by Nora and they get dad’s signature (at gunpoint and sadly not notarized - not sure if it will hold!) and they live happily ever after. Perhaps.
Notwithstanding it’s formulaic resolution, this film does provide a rare glimpse of queer life in Iran

title: ADULTHOOD
body:
While going through their mother’s home while she is in the hospital recovering from a stroke Meg and Noah accidentally discover the grisly remains of a neighbor who had disappeared 30 years earlier. Noah dissuades Meg from calling the police. He fears the relatives of the deceased will sue them and they will lose the family home. They dispose of the body in a local swamp only for it to be discovered and identified the very next day. More complications follow with a blackmail attempt and soon bodies start piling up.
To succeed, comedy noirs such as this require credible characters and a certain degree of plausibility which is sadly lacking here

title: BOUCHRA
body:
Co-directed by Israeli-born Orian Barki and Moroccan-born Meriem Bennani, this hybrid documentary/fiction debut animation feature explores the desire of a ‘real life’ and a fictional film maker both living in New York for their cardiologist (‘real life’)/artist (fictional) mothers both living in Casablanca to come to terms with the daughters’ lesbianism.  Actual recorded telephone conversations between the ‘real life’ Bouchra are played against (AI-generated?) 3D animation that imagines the two (and the daughters’ lesbian milieu) as hybrid humans with coyote and other animal heads. 
I wasn’t entirely enamoured of the very dark palette of the animation.  Yet I acknowledge that it elegantly complements the joyful and explicit scenes of lesbian sex portrayed.  The interplay between the fictional and ‘real-life’ film maker characters was at times confusing and not helped by the fact that both were called ‘Bouchra’.  That, together with the theme and the experimental nature of the film - while quite original - will probably limit it’s appeal to sophisticated LGBTQ audiences. 
3-

title: THE PRESIDENTS CAKE
body:
Young Lamia lives with her ailing impoverished grandmother in the marshes of 1990s Iraq when she is assigned, under penalty of severe retribution if she fails, to bake a cake (“big, filled with lots of cream”) for the mandatory school celebration of Saddam Hussein’s birthday. The film follows her on her odessey to secure the scarce ingredients for the cake her family cannot afford to make.  
Hasan Hadi’s moving debut feature, made entirely with an excellent cast of non-professionals premiered in Cannes earlier alongside the thematically very similar AMRUN by Fatih Akin, a film I very much loved.  (There, the boy was trying to secure white bread, butter and honey for his Nazi mother, who, grieving the Führer’s death, refused to eat anything else.) But while Hadi’s film garnered its deserved prizes, Akin’s more polished (and in my view more audience-pleasing) film seems to have been largely ignored. Both are worth catching.
4/5 <This message was edited>

title: THE UGLY
body: Dong-Hwan is working with his single father, a reknowned blind stamp carver, about whom a television crew is making a routine documentary segment, when the police discover the 40 year old remains of his long disappeared mother. The documentary filmmaker is intrigued and together with the son she seeks to discover what has happened to a woman so ugly, her colleagues named her ‘dung demon’. Yeong Sang-ho’s elegant thriller adroitly maintains tension as shameful memories are pealed and confronted. Recommended

title: STEVE
body:
Cillian Murphy reprises his collaboration with Belgian director Tim Mielants and fellow cast member Emily Watson with whom he worked on last year’s excellent SMALL THINGS LIKE THESE.  Here he plays the headmaster of an experimental publicly-funded boarding school for very troubled boys in 1996 Britain. Over 24 hours he and his team lurch from crisis to crisis with their  charges as they contend with an unruly crew of documentary filmmakers, a visiting Conservative politician and the sudden news that the school will be shut down in six months.  Naturally, it would take more than just great acting, in abundance here, to lift this often rehashed narrative trope. What really impresses is the brilliant camerawork: with one particularly memorable long, fluid, drone-propelled single take of interior then exterior then back to interior scenes which capture and reflect the prevailing chaos.  Netflix produced. Highly recommended.
4-

title: CALIFORNIA SCHEMIN
body:
Gavin and Billy were two rappers from Dundee who felt they were not taken seriously by London-based record companies because of their strong Scottish accents. Pretending to be Californians turned their fortunes.  This directoral debut from actor James McAvoy is a mildly entertaining but unremarkable retelling of their story. 
3/5 <This message was edited>

title: NUREMBERG
body:
Based on Jack El Hai’s non-fiction 2013 account, a US Army psychiatrist (Rami Malek) is brought in to evaluate the Nazi war criminals being prosecuted at Nuremberg. Chief among them is Herman Göring (Russell Crowe). The psychiatrist works with the prosecutors (Michael Shannon and Richard E. Grant) to help them anticipate Göring’s defence and to exploit his vanity to incriminate himself.  
Lesser directors and actors would have been tempted to portray the portly and pompous Göring as a ridiculous figure. To their credit Crowe is allowed to deliver a nuanced performance as someone who while cunning and manipulative comes across as being quite charismatic. An interesting coda, clearly intended to inject some present day relevance, reveals that the psychiatrist went on to publish in the 1950s a book about the Nazi war criminals. While promoting it, he argued that such characters could, given the opportunity, thrive even in America

title: ELEANOR THE GREAT
body:
ELEANOR THE GREAT (Opening night gala, Curzon Mayfair Thursday6/11 18:30)

https://www.festival-cannes.com/en/f/eleanor-the-great/
Best friends Bessie and Eleanor have been happily living together in Florida after their husbands died years ago.  When Bessie passes, Eleanor moves in with her divorced daughter and grandson in Manhattan.  Feeling bored and lonely, Eleanor accidentally stumbles on an holocaust survivor support group meeting at the Jewish Community Center.  There she tells her story.  Except Eleanor grew up in America and did not experience the holocaust… 
Scarlett Johansson’s comedy drama is elevated by the witty and sassy role of Eleanor, ably performed by June Squibb.  It was a little too sentimental for my taste but it is sure to please many audiences.
3/5 <This message was edited>

title: A LETTER TO DAVID
body:
https://www.berlinale.de/en/2025/programme/202505181.html
David and Eitan Cunio are twin brothers from Nir Oz in southern Israel.  Their parents emigrated from Argentina in the eighties seeking a Kibbutz socialist lifestyle.  Ten years ago, the brothers, both unprofessional actors, were cast in a drama directed by filmmaker Tom Shoval about two brothers who kidnap a girl for ransom to help their financially troubled family. Shoval was struck by the powerful real life bond of the brothers which he felt mirrored that of his characters.  On October 7th, David and younger brother Ariel were kidnapped and taken to Gaza, where they are languishing as of this writing (Sept 2025).  Eitan and his family barely survived as their house was set on fire by the Hamas terrorists as they hid in their strong room.  Using clips from the casting tapes, the 2004 drama and interviews with Eitan, his parents and David’s wife, Shoval provides an intimate and achingly painful portrait of the Cunios. Sadly, the Berlinale’s inclusion of this film attracted protests from pro-Palestinian groups. (https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/movies/movie-news/gaza-debate-returns-to-berlin-red-carpet-1236133126/) The tragedy of Gaza does not nullify this family’s suffering

title: PLUNDERER
body:
https://ukjewishfilm.org/event/plunderer-the-life-and-times-of-a-nazi-art-thief/

Bruno Lohse was a little-known art historian, until he was drafted into the German army and recruited by the Einsatzstab Reichsleiter Rosenberg (ERR): a Nazi unit tasked with looting art across Europe. Stationed in Paris, Lohse soon caught the eye of Hermann Göring, who commissioned him to source artworks for his personal collection. In Hugo Macgregor’s gripping documentary, historian, Jonathan Petropoulos — who met and filmed Lohse several times during his research — uncovers the astonishing story of how Lohse not only escaped justice after the war, but later profited from the postwar art market. As American museums sought to expand their collections, and art philanthropy became a lucrative method for tax mitigation, Lohse quietly trafficked the looted art. The film exposes the shadowy intersections between high art, war crimes, and postwar ambition, offering a chilling reminder of how plunder is the most profitable and least risky war crime

title: ALL I HAD WAS NOTHINGNESS
original_title: JE N’AVAIS QUE LE NÉANT - “SHOAH” PAR LANZMANN
body:
https://www.berlinale.de/en/2025/programme/202503264.html
Claude Lanzmann’s 9.5hr doc, SHOAH, was released in 1985, 12 years in the making.  Lanzmann interviewed victims, perpetrators and also these who lived close to the killing fields.  The result is considered by many as one of the most important documentaries ever made on any subject.  Lanzmann left over 220 hours of footage that was not used in his documentary and filmmaker Guillome Ribot uses these, with voiceover readings of Lanzmann’s memoirs and writings to reveal the process of the making of the documentary:  the fruitless search for funding in America, the subterfuge needed to get interviews with perpetrators, his long search for survivors and the process of working with them.  Fascinating for anyone interested in documentary fimmmaking and not just the holocaust

title: CUZ YOU’RE UGLY
body:
https://ukjewishfilm.org/event/cuz-youre-ugly-qa/
The morbidly obese and very abrasive Avigail is on a mission to lose her virginity on the weekend prior to joining an army officer training programme.  Her sister's unwanted pregnancy throws a wrench in the plan.  
Featuring superb performances by the two female leads, this exceptional comedy drama shines a critical light on contemporary militaristic Israeli society.   I was impressed by the director's effort to make Avigail initially as unlikable as possible and then turn the audience round with some very moving key scenes.  
4/5 <This message was edited>

title: KAFKA’S LAST TRIAL
body:
https://ukjewishfilm.org/event/kafkas-last-trial/
A fascinating documentary about an ironically Kafkaesque trial in Israel relating to Kafka’s literary inheritance

title: THE FIRST LADY
body:
https://ukjewishfilm.org/event/the-first-lady/
This is a personal favourite of mine.  I wrote the following to the folks at FICX:  If the combination of “documentary,” “trans woman,” and “Israeli” doesn’t scare you off, I encourage you to consider this hidden gem that has just won the first prize at Docaviv 25. It’s a moving portrait of Efrat Tilma, one of the first transgender women in Israel, who, inspired by Coccinelle, traveled to Paris and performed in her club, underwent surgery in Morocco, and eventually returned to Israel, where she volunteered as a police officer and later became an activist for trans rights in the struggle against Netanyahu’s government.

This inspiring, funny, and touching film doesn’t shy away from revealing the traumas and tragedies that affected Efrat and her peers. I can think of many friends in Gijón who would be deeply moved by this film, whose appeal goes well beyond an LGBTQ+ audience

title: A VOIX BASSE
body:
Eya Bouteraa’s apprehensive expression fills in the entire screen in the opening shot of Leyla Buozid’s competition drama.  She is Lilia, returning to Tunisia for her uncle’s funeral. After depositing her girlfriend in a hotel, she rushes to console her grandmother, mum and aunt, grieving the death of her uncle. 
It soon transpires that the deceased was a victim of a vicious homophobic attack, though it is evidently a matter of shame for the family who angrily shoe away the uncle’s ex-lover.  While the family is eager to have the uncle, his secrets and the investigation into his murder buried quickly, Lilia is keen to uncover her uncle’s past and the circumstances of his murder.  Buzoid maintains tension and pace as she adroitly examines the complex web of relationships between Laila, her girlfriend, her relatives and the uncle’s milieu and extracts superb performances from her cast with SUCCESSION’s Hiam Abbass meriting a special mention for her role as Laila’s mother.  Even the uncle, mostly presented in a series of wedding photographs that Laila finds in his closet, delivers a powerful emotional punch.  Highly recommended

title: HANGAR ROJO
body: Juan Pablo Sallato’s tight, elegant first full-length feature concerns the moral dilemma faced by real-life Chilean Air Force Captain Jorge Silva. One first day of the 1973 coup, his training school is taken over by an old nemesis to be used as a torture and interrogation centre for political prisoners. Sallato’s elegant monochrome camerawork follows and lingers on Nicolás Zárate’s hauntingly chiseled face as he ponders difficult choices.  Highly recommended

title: NO GOOD MEN
body: In the months prior to the American withdrawal, Naru and her friends at Kabul TV station are discussing why Afghan men are so horrible to their wives.  “Afghan men are traumatised,” claims one of them.  Naru doesn’t buy it.  “Afghan men are traumatised?  Afghan women are traumatised!”  Naru, a tv camerawoman is separated from her cheating husband but will not divorce him lest he take away their son.  She also has to contend with fairly vile sexism at work and only slowly sheds her distrust to develop an affectionate relationship with one of her male colleagues.  Spoiler alert.   There was one good man in Kabul after all!  Watchable but unremarkable selection for the festival’s opening night gala

title: ROSEBUSH PRUNING
body: Despite being a big fan of his previous, tropical noir, MOTEL DESTINO, I found Aïnouz’s latest too disgusting to sit through. Audiences that can stomach it, could soon do so on MUBI

title: PLAN CONTRAPLAN
body:
In 1986, the Jewish American photojournalist Edward Serotta traveled and captured images throughout Romania. Ceausescu was obsessed with paying off the country’s foreign debt making conditions in the country grim for all Romanians. Serotta was particularly interested in the life of the Jewish community and to the extent that it was possible (given the fear of locals to engage with him) he documented what he could.

The first part of this brief but fascinating documentary short is a slideshow of his monochrome stills with Seretta’s charming and chatty voiceover recollections. The second part is a no less fascinating reading of the Securitate (secret police) file of his visit illustrated by images they surreptitiously captured of Serrota.  It appears they took more pictures of him than he did during his visit. Moreover, it is apparent that some of the people Serrotta was talking to were secret police informants engaged in influencing his reporting. Highly recommended

title: EFFONDREMENT
body: As a young woman, Anat Evan lived in Kibbutz Nir Oz.  She had left years ago, but had maintained friendships with many former neighbours, many of whom were killed or kidnapped.  Shortly after the October 7th attack, she returns to her former home to witness the devastation there.  In the background are the sounds of fighter jets and explosions, an unprecedentedly savage Israeli response that she regards cruel war of vengeance, and one which she laments most Israelis choose to avert their eyes from.  Unable to enter Gaza, Evan and her camera rove around its perimeter, recording distant explosions while in voiceover she reads her correspondence with an anti-Zionist friend in Paris, a doctor and a mother in Gaza and calls on a munitions expert and an ornithologist to explain the explosive ground tremors she feels and the crazed behaviour of birds she records.  She visits Reim park, site of the Nova rave and massacre, where, she says, thousands of young Israelis partied, oblivious to the suffering across the border in Gaza.  Now that this blood soaked land has been turned into a memorial site and been planted with flags what is going to be its impact, she asks:  perpetuating rage and endless wars?  Ultimately, who is this film for?  As she appears to acknowledge, I do not think it will convince many Israelis, who would prefer not to listen.  Others, like her friend in Paris might feel her project irrelevant and possibly even self-indulgent

title: THE EDUCATION OF JANE CUMMINGS
body: In THE CELLULOID CLOSET, his seminal book about Hollywood, Vito Russo lamented the fate of gay and lesbian characters who often ended up dead. William Wyler’s 1961 THE CHILDREN’S HOUR, about two female teachers unjustly accused by one of their young students of lesbianism was one of the films he used to illustrate his thesis. Sophie Heldman’s elegant retelling of a similar (true) story, set in 1810 Scotland imbues the narrative with the added complexity of a racial dimension. Would it surprise you that the fate of its characters be just as grim?  Beautifully shot, designed and cast, this film is no less haunting. Highly recommended

title: ALLEGRO PASTELL
body: Watching paint dry would be more stimulating than this dull film about the ups and downs of a long distance relationship between two thirty year olds, a writer and a web developer

title: STAATSSCHUTZ
body:
“If only 80% of your cases are dismissed, you are doing ok,” one Seyo’s colleagues tells her after the case she is prosecuting against an ultra right criminal collapses.  But Seyo, a junior state prosecutor of Korean descent refuses to be consoled. Indeed, when that now freed perpetrator tries to burn her alive with an incendiary device she is absolutely livid!  Unsatisfied with her superior’s lacklustre handling of her case, she decides to hire her own private prosecutor and even sneak into the prosecution archives of dismissed cases to look for materials that might support her suspicions of official collusion with ultra right wing impunity.
I am a big fan of German political cinema of the late 70s and 80s. (Sorry, Wim, I am thinking more of your colleagues like Schlöndorff, Fassbinder and von Trotta.) So  I am glad to see Faraz Shariat continue the tradition. Almost fifty years on, the genre’s brutalist paranoid austerity has been refreshed with an almost cool as gherkin diminuitive heroine who drives a jet black sports car and scores bullseyes in the shooting range.  Recommended.
4/5 <This message was edited>

title: A FAMILY
body: In the film’s opening scene Nina and Eli read out personal statements to the judge who will determine their custody arrangements in their parents contentious divorce. We then see how their parents’ behavior impacts on them, with scenes - some overlaping - played out initially from Nina’s point of view and later from Eli’s. In this, his third feature, Peijnenburg draws out outstanding performances from his young cast. Highly recommended

title: WHO KILLED ALEX ODEH?
body:
The 1967 war caught Odeh at university in Cairo, thus preventing his return to the West Bank in its aftermath. Twenty years on he was the West Coast head of the Arab Anti Discrimination League. In that position he was involved with interfaith peace and reconciliation efforts. Indeed tv clips show Jewish community leaders mourning his passing as “someone who you could talk to about peace.”  In 1986, after the Achille Lauro cruise ship was hijacked by the PLO and a Jewish American passenger killed, Odeh was interviewed by local tv channels. His friends claim that his robust condemnation of the incident was edited out and airing just his statement that he “understood the desperation and motivations”of the perpetrators. The next day a pipe bomb killed him.  In this doc, Israeli journalist David Shin follows on the work of others to try to discover, 40 years on, who killed him and why they haven’t been brought to justice.  Spoiler alert: according to them probably JDL activists, including Itamar Ben Gvir former law firm boss. Guess where these people are today…  Interesting doc, rich with tv clips, interviews with suspects, informants and former investigators that seeks to show how we have ended where we are. 
3-

title: WHERE TO
body:
Hassan, a Palestinian share-ride driver in Berlin picks up handsome young Israeli gay man Amir (Ido Tako of THE VANISHING SOLDIER) and his date outside a Berlin nightclub. Over the next several months they run into each other again. One night Hassan notices Amir, drunk and despondent over his recent breakup outside a club and takes him to Amir’s home. “Have you ever been in love?” Asks Amir on the way. This question sparks Hassan’s search and reckoning with his own romantic tragedy.  A sweet hidden gem of a film, strongest when no one says a word and we are left with the gently observed expressions that reveal everything.  
Israelis and Palestinians will be particularly amused by a brief scene that accurately captures the panic of Israeli tourists when they hear their driver speak Arabic and see the small Palestinian flag hanging from his mirror.  Given the cultural boycott, this film which was probably only accepted in Berlin due to being set here, is unlikely to make it outside Israeli cinemas and Jewish film festivals. A pity

title: QUEEN AT SEA
body:
When Amanda makes an unannounced visit to check on her demented mother and stepfather, she is furious to find them having sex. This is not the first time and Amanda feels her mother lacks the capacity to give consent. When the stepfather refuses to promise he will desist, Amanda calls the police. This sets off a cascading sequence of events, some expected and unexpected.  This intelligent, thought provoking and beautifully observed film features powerful performances by Juliette Binoche as Amanda and Tom Courtney as the stepfather.  It is not perfect, though. I did not find the inclusion of a tangential story of Amanda’s daughter’s sexual awakening a convincing counterpoint to the relationship between the elderly couple.  Still it’s highly recommended.
4/5 <This message was edited>

title: HEYSEL 85
body: In May 1985, Heysel stadium in Brussels hosted a cup final between Liverpool and Juventus. Before the game started, rioting English fans stormed a neighbouring ‘neutral’ section where there were many Juventus fans.  In the stampede 35 fans died and hundreds were injured.  To avoid the riot to spreading to the city, a decision was made to hold the game anyway.  It appears that this situation could have been foreseen and averted by the authorities.  Teodora Ana Mihai  blends tv clips from the time with her dramatised scenes to tell this story of official chaos and incompetence mainly through two characters:  the municipality’s press officer (who also was the mayor’s daughter) and an Italian TV journalist.  Watchable but unremarkable

title: ROSE
body: Germans are masters of feminist period movies where transgressors are met with severe punishment.  I am thinking of DES TEUFELS BAD and THE GIRL WITH THE NEEDLE.  (Ok, the last one was Danish/Polish, but they are neighbors!). Markus Schleinzer’s new film shares with the others it’s atmospheric monochrome cinematography and Grimm-brothers moralistic/sadistic storytelling.  I had to look up poena cullei though thanksfully we are spared seeing it.  Sandra Hüller is terrific as the soldier who returns to his village to reclaim his inheritance.  Highly recommended

title: TRULY NAKED
body: For once I can state that the Berlinale program summary does a good job of describing the narrative and theme of this film. What blew me away was the intelligence, empathy and originality with which it treats porn and its impact on its creators and consumers

title: TAKE ME HOME
body:
Korean American Liz Sargent and her cognitively disabled sister Anna were both adopted and raised by a midwestern family.  In this largely autobiographical independent first feature, Liz directs her sister and actors that play her parents and a character based on a ‘normal’ sister.
As one of the parents passes, the other parent’s increasing dementia and the limits of the ‘normal’ sister’s ability to help become evident, the choices facing the family in a country with poor publicly funded safety nets are very grim.  The final scenes of Anna flourishing in an idyllic institution are utopian, what “could and should happen”, according to Liz in the Q&A.  Sadly this clarification was necessary for me and other Berlinale audiences. 
‘Directing Anna’ is a bit of a stretch.  The brave choice of casting a severely cognitively disabled person as herself required a flexible approach. Most scenes had to develop and evolve around Anna’s limitations and the actors had adapt themselves to the situations.  The largely successful result has an authenticity lacking from less gritty films that employ ‘normal’ actors in roles such as Anna’s.  Recommended

title: CHICAS TRISTES
body: Fernanda Tovar’s first time feature concerns two friends, members of a high school swimming team, one of whom is raped by another team member.  The excellent performances of the two young leads feel authentic and the film’s treatment of the important and topical theme sensitive. Nevertheless, the languid pacing, with long underwater pool scenes and the unnecessary inclusion of a couple of tangential characters make the film feel much longer than its 90 minutes. The morally anticlimactic, though perhaps realistic conclusion may also frustrate some audiences

title: LES JUIFS RICHES
body:
I find documentary filmmaker Yolande Zauberman’s themes and her treatment of them fascinating: an ultra orthodox man confronting the rabbi that abused him as a child (M), Palestinian trans sex workers in Tel Aviv (LA BELLE DE GAZA). This short is no exception. Thankfully, though, we are spared Zauberman’s sea-sickness inducing handheld camerawork as this film is composed entirely of old home movies:  a bar mitzvah, wedding, circumcision ceremony featuring her relatives whose brave and sometímes shocking stories of wartime survival Zauberman shares. Interspersed are sad Jewish jokes. A man goes to his rabbi.  “I want to kill myself,” he tells the rabbi. “That is not the solution,” responds the rabbi. “What is the solution?” 
“Who said there was a solution!” Answers the rabbi.  Recommended.

title: MOSCAS
body: A curmudgeon lonely woman reluctantly takes on a short term tenant in order to pay for a procedure on an ingrown toenail.  The man, whose wife is  a patient in the hospital next door sneaks his son into the room at night and takes him out every morning.  The 9 year old boy is soon discovered and slowly charms his way into the landlady’s heart.  This charming Mexican film, quite reminiscent of CENTRAL STATION, has its own original touches of magical realism and delves into sentimentality without being too saccharine

title: GELBE BRIEFE
body:
Actress Derya is annoyed by the gentleman in the centre stalls at her play’s premiere in Ankara’s National Theatre whose phone keeps ringing.  Afterwards, when he requests that she pose for a picture with him, she refuses. The next day the play is cancelled and she is fired. Her husband Aziz, the play’s writer and a university professor is fired along with colleagues for their stand ‘against the war’ and is charged with abetting terrorism and insulting the President.  The duo and their 14 year old daughter decamp to Istanbul to move in to Derya’s mother’s cramped apartment where the pressures on the family keep rising.
İlker Çatak follows his excellent THE TEACHERS’ LOUNGE with this intelligent and powerful drama about a family under an authoritarian state’s attack. To underscore the universality of the theme, Çatak employs multiple specifics, ambiguously.  The film’s title, ‘Yellow Letters’, with which the protagonists receive their summons or notices of termination, in Germany refer to official, legally binding documents from courts or government authorities that are delivered with proof of service. They are considered extremely important and must not be ignored. Section titles ‘Berlin for Ankara’ and ‘Hamburg for Istanbul’ underscore that the scenes are shot in Germany.  There are references to the Kurdish national struggle (and presumably Turkey’s wars against them) but in demonstrations at the University we also see Ukrainian, Palestinian and Rainbow flags.  And while Çatak’s sympathy for his protagonists is undeniable, he does not shy from exposing their personal shortcomings. Highly recommended

title: THE ONLY LIVING PICKPOCKET IN NEW YORK
body:
It’s hard being an analogue era pickpocket in the digital age. Most people hardly carry cash and so many of them wear crap fake watches. But Harry gets by and even manages to take care of his catatonic wife. One day, however, he steals from the wrong guy…
This delightfully enjoyable, old fashioned New York crime drama features great performances from some old hands: the wonderful John Torturo, Steve Buscemi and Giancarlo Esposito. Great audience pleaser

title: KURTULUŞ
body:
Emin Alper’s deserving Berlinale Silver Bear winner is apparently based on real events. But like it’s Golden Bear winning counterpart, GELBE BRIEFE, it has aspirations for broader relevance. It concerns a land feud between two clans in deep Anatolya: one that escalates and eventually results in a genocidal massacre. (One would find parallels with many ethnic conflicts: Hutu/Tutsi in Rwanda/Congo/DRC for example.)  
While it definitely is a worthy film and one that kept me at the edge of my seat, I hesitate to recommend it for FICX. It is a challenging film to follow. Even I, who speaks some Turkish found it hard to keep up with some characters and threads. It was also difficult to decipher reality from the main character’s dreams and visions. (Probably it was hard for him too!!) Yet the scenes in the mosque, with the men shaking their heads in unison to and fro to the beating of drums as they worked themselves into a religious frenzy, will linger

title: NINA ROZA
body:
Michel has been living in Montreal for the past 26 years. While his art gallery boss is enthusiastic about an 8-year old art prodigy in his native Bulgaria, Michel is skeptical.  There are many scammers out there.  Reluctantly he agrees to his boss’s request that he go and check this girl out for himself.  What starts as an investigation soon evolves into a voyage into his own past and regrets.
This slow, contemplative film won the Berlinale’s competition best screenplay prize but despite its 100 minutes failed to engage and convince me. Sorry

title: NARCISO
body:
The last Paraguayan film I saw was Marcelo Martinessi’s wonderful 2018 LAS HEREDERAS, a darkly atmospheric portrait of two ageing lesbians in Asunción.  Sadly I am not as enthusiastic about his latest film which is also set in that town and also appears to be shot almost entirely at night. It is 1959 and Alfredo Stroessner’s brutal 40 year dictatorship is just beginning. Handsome and sultry Narciso is a DJ who introduces rock and roll music to the traditional folk-music radio station he joins.  His show is wildly popular but the regime considers rock and roll degenerate and contributing to the moral corruption of the nation’s youth.
Narciso not only appeals to the young and not so young women of Paraguay, he also turns the heads of men, such as the closeted station’s owner and a creepy American hydro engineer played by Nahuel Perez Biscayart (120 BPM). The engineer, who speaks Spanish with a weirdly unconvincing American accent, is engaged on a project to bring drinking water to the capital.  Yet, for some unexplained reason, is regularly invited as a guest on the station’s shows.  With more than a nod to Polanski’s CHINATOWN, the inauguration of the hydro project is soon followed by the death of Narciso in a mysterious fire.  This is blamed on degenerate elements and sets off a massive anti-gay persecution.  
Umh…. It looks good and won Fipresci Panorama jury award, but left me unconvinced

title: 277999.HTML.
body:
And that’s it from Berlin.  After taking Saturday off to visit Dresden, I returned yesterday for a marathon four movies. In all I saw 22 full length features of which 15 were good or very good.  I would consider this an excellent result. Hope you get to see some of these soon. I would love to know what you think of them.

Of the main competition my favourites were 
GELBE BRIEFE
QUEEN AT SEA 
A VOIX BASSE
ROSE

In the Panorama/Perspectives my top choices were 
TRULY NAKED
A FAMILY
WHERE TO
ISABEL

A full list of the festival award winners appears here:  https://www.berlinale.de/en/2026/news-press-releases/277999.html.
My next festival is in Cannes and will take place in May.   Big hugs until then. See you at the movíes!

title: NOVEMBER 1963
body:
This political conspiracy thriller by Roland Joffe aims to explain President JFK’s assassination. In a 1979 preamble, John Travolta’s character who is due to testify before a congressional committee, explains that JFK’s father made a deal with the Mafia to help get his son elected in return to having a ‘friendly’ President in office. Instead, the President’s brother, Attorney General Robert Kennedy, began to aggressively prosecute them.  Enraged by this betrayal, the Mafia decided to kill the President. The facile manner this explanation is presented and the tedious arrangements to set up the assassination in the long flashback that follows, drain the first half of the film from any tension. It is only after the President is shot and things go very wrong that the film begins to pick up rhythm. Features a good performance by John Travolta. Very watchable, but this film won’t won’t dethrone Pakula, Coppola or Rosi from their perch as the kings of this genre.
3/5 <This message was edited>

title: DUA
body:
Thirteen year old Dua has to contends with typical teenage girl troubles: a changing body, boys, some bitchy classmates. Except that these are the late 90s in Kosovo and tensions between the ruling Serbs and Dua’s ethnic Albanian community are rising. When her friend’s sister is found dead and she is groped by menacing Serb neighbour, Dua decides to join classmate Mika’s judo class…
Pinea Matoshi as Dua leads a stellar cast, in this beautifully observed second feature by Blerta Basholli

title: IN WAVES
body: Chosen as the opening film of the Semaine de la Critique section, Phuong Mai Nguyen’s first feature is an animated melodrama about the relationship between a 16 year old Californian skateboarder and a his surfer girlfriend. Their romance is tragically interrupted by her illness.  It is very much the case here that the way their story is told is much more important than the narrative itself. Gorgeously animated with restrained sentimentality and just the right amount of magical realism the medium allows. Recommended

title: WE ARE ALIENS
body: Another beautifully animated feature with some truly amazing visuals. This one concerns a Japanese taxi driver that reminisces about his childhood and coming of age. Sadly, it keeps flicking across time periods and actual (and imagined/dreamt about?) realities that I soon lost the plot. It’s one of these films where I will need to wait a day for the more clever reviewers in SCREEN or THE HOLLYWOOD REPORTER to explain to me what I have seen. Or maybe not

title: VIVA
body:
In this film’s opening shot we see Ana’s one remaining breast uncomfortably clamped to a medical imaging device. There is a small lump there, she is told. It might be benign but with her history, a needle biopsy is advisable.  Not now, decides Ana and keeps dodging the oncologist‘s calls.  She is in a hurry to Live Her Life.  Living, for medical researcher Ana includes dumping her longtime partner and embarking on a hot affair with a sexy dancer half her age…
There is a lot to commend Aina Cotlet’s directorial debut, including her own performance as the heroine, Cotlet’s unflinching exposition of her own scarred body and the joy she takes in the pursuit of sexual pleasure. (One fellatio scene must rank as one of the most memorable in the history of cinema.) But while I wanted to love this film, I ended up just liking it.  I can’t put my finger on exactly why. But I couldn’t help compare it to Isabel Coixet’s superb THREE GOODBYES (TIFF 2025) which covers similar dramatic territory

title: FORESAKEN
body:
Samuel Paty was a French secondary school teacher.  In October 2020, during a civics class on the conflict between free expression and religious intolerance, he showed his class the blasphemous cartoons published in the satirical magazine CHARLIE HEBDO a few years earlier, which provoked the massacre of that magazine’s staff a few years earlier.  In consideration of the sensabilities of those who might take offense, he invited them to absent themselves from the class for a few minutes while these cartoons were projected.  A student who was absent from the class and had been suspended for unrelated issues, lied to her father and accused Paty and the school of racism.  The enraged father, goaded by an Islamic agitator, launched a social media campaign against the teacher and the school.  Eleven days later, while on his way home, Paty was killed on the streets outside the school by an Islamist Russian immigrant of Chechen descent who livestreamed his decapitation.
This gripping film follows the last days of Paty’s life and asks thought provoking questions about the limits of freedom of speech, the impact of social media in amplifying lies and the systemic failures that led to Paty’s death. Highly recommended

title: A WOMAN’S LIFE
body: Fiftyfive year old Gabrielle’s life is in a funk. The work pressures at the public hospital where she heads an oral surgery unit are growing as colleagues abandon to work in the private sector.
