The annoying grown up kids of her long time partner are refusing to leave the family home and the relationship with him is sort of stale anyway. Her selfish mother is rapidly declining and will soon have to be moved into a care home. And then she falls for the novelist who is tasked with shadowing her at work. Léa Drucker’s considerable talents are wasted in this routine lacklustre French drama and Cannes competition entry. Give it a pass

title: FATHERLAND
body: Pawel Pawlikowski’s atmospheric literary drama in luscious monochrome follows Thomas Mann and his daughter Erika on a 1949 road trip from exile in California to receive the Goethe prize, actually two: one in Frankfurt and one in the east in Russian occupied Weimar. They learn of Erika’s brother Klaus’s suicide. There is a testy encounter between Erika and her ex-husband and Klaus’s ex-lover actor Gustaf Gründrings, who inspired Klaus’s novel MEPHISTO. (Erika’s other husband WH Auden was also gay.)  Erika grieves. Thomas apparently doesn’t. She complains about the ex-Nazis that are now feteing her father. Thomas delivers speeches and politely declines an invitation to become an East German cultural commissar.  A man who breaks into their hotel suite to protest political imprisonment by Soviets in nearby Buchenwald is brusquely removed by the secret police. And that’s basically it. Left me rather flat

title: CLUB KID
body:
In his debut feature as director, Jordan Firstman plays a burned out gay club party promoter into whose lap the 10 year old son he never knew he had is dumped.  
The narrative formula of suddenly introducing a cute kid into the messy life of a crusty character has been explored some times before.  John Cassavettes’s GLORIA, with his wife Gena Rowlands playing a a hardened mafia moll reluctantly saving a small kid on whose life a contract was issued, is a favourite of mine.  So while this is formulaic, I must admit I am a sucker for this formula.  Firstman manages to balance humour, pathos and disbelief suspension to a reasonable degree and to almost keep sentimentality and excess cutesiness in check.  Easily the most enjoyable film I saw so far in Cannes this year

title: ALL OF A SUDDEN
body:
Marie-Luo is the director of a care home introducing her skeptical staff to more humane methods of caring for their charges. One evening she meets Mari, a terminally ill experimental theatre director.  The film follows their brief and intense friendship. Over the film’s 196 minutes they discuss many subjects that fascinate them like, for example, capitalism’s impact on birth rates and ageing population and the prospects for democracy. There are a few powerfull moments in Hamaguchi’s Cannes Competition entry, but frankly I would have not sat through the entire screening had I not been trapped in the middle of Grand Theatre Lumière’s dangerously vertiginous balcony section.
2/5 <This message was edited>

title: SHANA
body:
Twentysomething Shana’s life is a mess!  She picks fights with her friends, her mother - who disapproves of her lip filling treatments and wants to split up with her abusive pusher boyfriend when he gets out of jail. In the meantime, she deals for him and occasionally dips into the proceeds (with predictable consequences in due course.) There are multiple references to Shana’s Jewish origins (“but I am against Israel and for Palestine,” she reassures a friend.) Director Lila Pinell attempts  to structure this film around the plagues of the Passover Haggadah, some of which Shana experiences, in a way that feels forced on the narrative. Likewise, the tone of the film remains uncertain- very gently comic at times - but perhaps not enough so. Ultimately, it’s  success depends on its ability to generate audience empathy for its heroine.  With me, at least, it failed. 
2/5 <This message was edited>

title: THINK GOOD
body: Gil, a production assistant, is impregnated by Jacques, an orthodox Jewish man. They hide this from a rabbi in Dubai and persuade him to marry them promptly.  Jacques’s jealous and manipulative nature soon comes to the fore and Gil is trapped in an increasingly abusive relationship. The film is split into chapters bookended by mikveh purification rituals that Gil schedules after menstruation, rituals that require careful preparation. As an act of defiance on her final visit, Gil decides to leave the mikveh before immersing in it. When she turns to the rabbi, he initially counsels reconciliation but when confronted with Gil’s ‘catalogue of grievances’ as he initially calls the list she hands him, he concludes that she should not feel trapped by her faith and that she should leave her husband. It is a sad reflection of contemporary Jewish life that the French mikvehs Gil visits are guarded by armed soldiers

title: THE MELTDOWN
body:
Although Chileans had just voted to end Pinochet’s brutal dictatorship, in 1992 he remains the head of the armed forces and is yet to be arrested in London. Disappearances are a taboo subject and a culture of secrecy and lies prevails.  Nine year old Ines, living in her grandparents’ hotel, befriends guest Hannah, a 15 year old skier from Germany who one day disappears. What Ines knows has better be kept from Hannah’s frantic mother…
Veteran director and screenwriter Manuela Martelli made a good choice to focus on Ines as the principal character of this slow burning drama though her film would benefit from tighter editing and better pacing.
3.5/5 <This message was edited>

title: THE VISITATION
body:
Veteran Director Volker Schlöndorff attempts to tell Germany’s 20th century history through the lives of four families that lived on one lakeside property not far from Berlin.
When Klara, the village mayor’s eldest daughter is impregnated by the local fisherman, he disinherits her and sells the plot to two families: an architect who buys it for his former assistant and lover with whom he plans to share a home and a Jewish family of textile manufacturers. During the Nazi period, the architect agrees to buy the Jewish family’s share at half the market value from the Jewish grandfather. The patriarch wants to pay for his daughter’s family’s emigration to South Africa. After the war, the architect and his wife escape to the west and their property is occupied by the family of a communist writer returning from exile in the Soviet Union. One day, the writer’s granddaughter finds the hidden, unanswered letters that the Jewish family’s granddaughter wrote to her grandparents who had “moved to Poland.” After the fall of the wall, the architect’s wife’s relatives reclaim the property from the Cummunist writer’s granddaughter in order to resell it at market value.  
Obviously, the sweeping epic nature of this elegant and accomplished masterwork limits how much Schlöndorff can do with each character but he does manage to insert a lot of telling details. For example, the architect complains about the 6% tax the government assesses on the difference between market value and the amount paid for Jewish property. His modernist ideas on the rebuilding of Berlin are rejected by Speer .(This rejection letter later saves him from persecution from the new Communist authorities of the DDR), but he is commissioned to design barracks for concentration camps. The communist writes about her fear of arrests that happened at night. “No, it was not by the Nazis,” she tells her granddaughter, obviously alluding to the exile in Stalin’s Russia.  Highly recommended

title: GENTLE MONSTER
body:
Musician Lucy’s world is upturned when police show up with a search warrant at the home she shares with her husband Philip and young son. The police are concerned with Philip’s online activities. Marie Kreutzer draws a powerful performance from Lea Seydoux, as the woman struggling to make sense of her relationship with a husband and with her fears about what may have happened to her son. A secondary narrative thread about the investigating policewoman’s problems with a demented father who keeps sexually harassing his carer detracts from this otherwise solid competition entry.

title: THE BELOVED
body:
The dramatic territory of a relationship between an absent film director father and his actress daughter was explored last year in Joachim Trier’s SENTIMENTAL VALUE. This film’s theme is similar. Though Sorogoyen’s is better. Much better.  The shattering performances from Bardem and Luengo that feel raw and genuine are in no small measure due to Sorogoyen. For instance, the film preamble is a first encounter in 13 years between father and daughter. In this 20 minute restaurant scene, he proposes her a part in his new film. This was shot over one day with no preparation for the actors and no rehearsals. In fact they didn’t even meet before the shooting. The film is not just about the relationship between the two. The creative process and the toll it can extract from its makers are unsparingly examined. 
Bardem’s character quotes Liv Ullmann about how closeups impact acting. Sorogoyen is a good student.  He uses multiple formats: digital, 35mm, 16mm, Super8, color, monochrome and switches constantly between them, even within one scene, for no discernible reason. When I read about it prior to the screening I was weary it might feel gimmicky and spurious. Strangely, it wasn’t jarring at all and appeared to compliment the raw texture of the emotions. Very highly recommended.

title: WHEN THE NIGHT FALLS
body:
In 1942, the Vichy government decreed that all Jewish refugees who had arrived in France after 1936 must be rounded up and deported to Paris, in the Nazi occupied zone. Despite his superiors’ suspicions about his excessive humanitarian zeal, Gilbert Lesege, a civil servant, volunteers to head a commission to review deportees’ eligibility for exception on 11 grounds (pregnancy, prior army service, unaccompanied minors etc.) He reluctantly accepts Father Alexandre Glasberg on the commission. Glasberg, a Jewish refugee from Ukrainian pogroms who had converted to Catholicism after arriving in France, runs a church based NGO whose principal activity appears to be fabrication of fake documents and placement of Jewish children. His activities are known to and (barely) tolerated by the Cardinal, a friend of Petain.  Over three days the commission meets at the temporary internment camp. Arguments ensue with the police superintendent, another member of the commission, demanding evidence for Glasberg’s numerous exemption petitions. Ultimately, the commission’s decisions are irrelevant and Lesege is informed that at midnight everyone will be deported, exempt or not. He and Glasberg decide to try to at least save the children. 
This is obviously a very heartfelt project for Daniel Auteuil, in his directoral debut, who also cowrote the script (based on actual events) and stars as Glasberg. Antoine Reinarts, as Lesage, delivers a nuanced performance as a man torn between his loyalty to his superiors and his Quaker convictions. Commendably, Lesage’s superiors and his police colleague are not portrayed as rabid antisemites but merely as functionaries motivated either by fear or belief that a defeated France can no longer host foreign refugees. In the film’s powerful and poignant climax, Lesege and Glasberg scramble through the refugees as they are being herded into waiting busses, urging them to sign away their children over to the care of the Church. Highly recommended.

title: GARANCE
body: Jeanne Herry’s competition entry is a  portrait of an underemployed Parisian actress descent into alcoholism. Adèle Exachopoulos is allowed to portray a complex and rounded character while thankfully spared the tedious relapse phase common to almost all addiction genre movies. Recommended

title: MOULIN
body:
László Nemes returns to Cannes with a dark and atmospheric competition entry on French resistance leader Jean Moulin. Shortly after returning to occupied France from London with the aim of uniting the various sparring units of the resistance, Moulin is rounded up at a meeting of resistance leaders and brought into the untender care of Lyon Gestapo head Klaus Barbie. Moulin insists that he was there by accident. But Barbie, played with obvious relish by Lars Eidinger (who must be 21st century cinema’s Nazi par excellence), does not believe him. The film’s most powerful scenes are the cat and mouse games the two play prior to the inevitable descent into torture. Thence on things become very ugly and uncomfortable for Moulin - and the audience.
The resistance genre’s masterwork remains JP Melville ‘s L’ARMEE DES OMBRES which is an obvious inspiration for this film. Gilles Lelouch’s cool performance as Moulin is very reminiscent of Lino Ventura’s as Gerbier in the earlier film.  But I do miss the character played by the wonderful Simone Signoret, as Gerbier sidekick. Recommended

title: JIM QUEEN
body: This charming and cheeky LGBT animated feature about a muscle queen and his twink admirer seeking a cure for a virus that is turning Paris gay men straight had the audience and me in stitches

title: STRAWBERRIES
body: Laïla Marrakchi’s raw and powerful third feature centres on the friendship of two Moroccan migrant laborers picking strawberries in Almeria. In the initial scene, when Hasna applies for her contract she is told that she requires to present evidence of her husband’s consent. This sets the tone for the challenges that follow: wage theft, abuse and undignified working conditions in Spain on the one hand and the expectations of the repressive patriarchal society they will have to return to. Through a carefully calibrated script and great performances from her cast, we are given to appreciate how easily things can be twisted to make their grievances dismissable and how easily justice can be denied despite their courage and perseverance. Recommended

title: WOMEN ON TRIAL
body:
In 1972, 16 year old rape victim Marie-Claire and her single working class mother were prosecuted for an committing (and aiding her) abortion. While there was no dispute on the facts, they were defended by feminist lawyer Gisèle Hailimi who wanted to use their trial  to campaign against anti-abortion laws.
This watchable but relatively unremarkable movie mostly focuses on how Hailimi prepares and conducts the trial.  Campaigning feel-good movies of this type usually succeed when audiences can identify with sympathetic heroes. Sadly, in Charlotte Gainsbourg’s performance, she comes across as quite abrasive and unlikable

title: PAPER TIGER
body: Queens, NY, 1986. Ex-policeman now successful security consultant Gary shows up at his engineer brother’s Irwin suburban family home with an exciting business proposal.  Why not start a consulting firm to assist the new Russian owned businesses that are now developing a foresaken part of the city?  His brother is initially weary.  City developments are controlled by the mafia, he says. Straight businesses stand no chance.  “The Russians are different,” assures him Gary, “they run legitimate businesses that just require regulatory guidance and there is a lot of money in providing that.”  Well, not quite, it appears. Terrific performances abound in James Gray tense competition entry thriller/family drama.  Highly recommended

title: I’LL BE GONE IN JUNE
body: “Why Los Cruces,” asks the foster parent that picks up 16 year old German exchange student Franny up  at the airport. “It was a lottery.” Thus begins her year in this sleepy New Mexican backwater.  Awkward at first, easy going Franny navigates the cultural differences and oddities of an America reeling from the Sept 11 attacks, she develops  friendships and falls in love with the handsome and brooding Elliott, someone she is warned about.  Like the charming and open Franny (played by with naturalistic authenticity by first time actress Naomy Cosma) this tender debut feature by Katharina Rivlis slowly wins our hearts.  Producer Wim Wenders’ non-judgemental love of the American West and its people is evident throughout

title: A MAN OF HIS TIME
body: An opportunistic self-styled management and efficiency expert tries to finagle a job in the new Vichy administration in this unfunny French comedy. It borrows much from THE OFFICE TV series including ridiculous monologues, absurd humiliations (such as agreeing to smuggle a Vichy minister’s cat across the demarcation line in return for a recommendation) and these trademark takes with continuous zoom adjustments. Looks strictly intended for the domestic market. (I summoned the courage to brave exiting Grand Theatre Lumiere’s vertiginous balcony in the dark after an hour.)

title: IRON BOY
body:
Ten year old Christophe, from a French farming family, is diagnosed with scoliosis, a curved spine condition, that necessitates wearing an iron corset.  A great story line, beautiful animation, sound design and editing make this a appealing feature for children and adults alike. Recommended.

title: LA BATAILLE DE GAULE: L’ÂGE DE FER
body:
In Antonin Baudry’s epic historical biopic De Gaulle comes across initially as quite a delusional quixotic character. Despite being regarded as such by at turns a skeptical/pragmatic/desperate Winston Churchill, he manages to engender a certain empathy and admiration from the British prime minister. On two occasions, the sidelined De Gaulle is brought back by stroke of luck and the strength of his perseverance. Hugely enjoyable patriotic fest with just the right amount of audience-pleasing humor. Highly recommended.

title: THE MAN I LOVE
body: Jimmy, an off-off-broadway actor, is preparing for his new play. Ira Sachs returns to late 80s AIDS ravaged New York (where his last film, the disappointing PETER HUJAR’S DAY was set) for this tenderly observed heartfelt drama which accurately captures these fraught times. Rami Malek returns to his BOHEMIAN RHAPSODY form to deliver another outstanding performance. Highly recommended

title: COWARD
body: Pierre is a young Belgian WW1 recruit.  In between the backbreaking work of transferring artillery shells to the front and retrieving the dead and wounded, he and his comrades are entertained by an crossdressing army troupe known as ‘the rejects’. Pierre catches the eye of the leader of that troupe.  Lukas Dhont, whose previous film was the terrific CLOSE, intelligently and sensitively directs the burgeoning intimacy between two completely inexperienced turn of the century men. Thankfully, the outcome is not as dark as CLOSE while suspension of disbelief is not compromised. Highly recommended

title: LA BOLA NEGRA
body:
Three narrative threads are weaved in Calvo and Ambrosi’s ambitious drama.  The first imagines Lorca’s last known work written shortly before his execution, an unfinished queer novel of which only four pages are believed to have been written, as a completed play of which only four pages have been found. The second follows a reluctant nationalist soldier who guards Lorca’s wounded lover and into whose hands the manuscript is entrusted. The third follows the soldier’s grandson, a historian and failed novelist living with his boyfriend in contemporary Madrid, who inherits the missing pages. 
It is a demanding watch. Knowledge of the above is helpful in following the twists of the threaded narratives but ultimately the impact is greater than the parts and hugely satisfying. Highly recommended

title: ATONEMENT
body:
In a London retrospective of his films, veteran Israeli director Eran Riklis (READING LOLITA IN TEHRAN) revealed that his next project will be a post October 7 drama on PTSD. “Every week in Israel a soldier who served in Gaza blows his own brain out,” he said.
PTSD trauma is the theme of Reed Van Dyk third feature starring Riklis’s friend and collaborator Palestinian actress Hiam Abbass (SUCCESSION). In 2003, an Iraqi family fleeing their bombed out home accidentally drive into an intersection where American forces are under insurgent fire. Fearing that the cars heading towards them are hostile, the soldiers shoot and kill the patriarch and two of his sons.  
Ten years on, deeply traumatized Michael, one of the soldiers, wishes to meet the surviving mother and daughter who now live in California. 
Why should the two rightfully apprehensive women want to relive their own traumas in order to help the man who is responsible for their own ongoing suffering? And why should the audience care?  It is to Van Dyk’s and his cast’s credit that these questions are painfully and honestly addressed.  As Michael’s partner says, “when you pick up a gun and shoot someone, the bullet travels both ways.” Recommended

title: ULYSSE
body:
A year after Ulysse is born, Alice begins to worry about that the baby does not crawl, consume anything other than milk or verbally communicate. Eventually, she and her husband receive a diagnosis:  Noonan syndrome. Thus begins the trio’s difficult journey through the challenges of bringing up a child and growing up with severe developmental deficits.  The marriage fails and institutional support is scant and inconsistent but ultimately, by sheer force of the mother’s perseverance and encouragement of her son, things work out.
Masson’s film has its heart in the right place and will continue to inspire parents for years to come. Special mention should be made of her masterly direction of the three boys playing Ulysse at various stages of his upbringing. Recommended

title: HOPE
body:
Every year the Cannes competition features a Hollywood blockbuster. This year the studios have deserted Cannes. (The few Us titles are indies or ‘small’ pics.) According to what I have read, the California ‘suites’ have concluded that May is too early to promote films that will be released in the autumn, when Cinéma going peaks.  That spot has been cheerfully grabbed by the Koreans.
For the 160 minutes of Na Hong Jin’s competition entry, alien monsters run on a rumpage through the Korean countryside in what feels like a tediously overlong video game. The inconclusive ending shamelessly leaves an opening for a sequel, as it inevitably must. Avoid

title: MINOTAUR
body:
A disturbing trend in cinema identified by my friend José Montaño, an experimental filmmaker from the age of celluloid is ‘image vacuuming’. Since digital capture is so much cheaper, filmmakers have lost discipline and are accumulating huge amounts of material that they can sift later through in the editing suite. (Discipline does not necessarily preclude spontaneity. John Cassavettes often kept a 1:1/1:2 shooting to finished film ratio and often used just a script outline.) I checked the average length of Cannes competition titles. It has risen from 113m in 2006 to 137m in 2026.  Guess what? Making films longer does NOT necessarily make them better.
Sadly, this lesson is clearly lost on Andreï Zviaguintsev. His 140m competition entry about a Russian business executive, whose wife cheats on him and whose personal moral corruption is a metaphor for his country’s, could have been a superb 90m film. Sadly, it isn’t

title: FJORD
body: Romanian director Cristian Mongiu who won the 2007 Palme d’Or for his excellent abortion drama 4 MONTHS, 2 WEEKS, 3 DAYS, returns with this excellent drama that pits a religiously conservative Romanian immigrant family against the might of the Norwegian child protection services. Some might feel that Mongiu depiction of Norwegian progressive intolerance is a tad heavy handed (a teacher reports the family when their daughter tells a lesbian classmate that “lesbianism is wrong”and the prosecutor in a trial to decide the fate of the family’s children appears to be putting the parents’ religious convictions on trial,) but I didn’t feel it detracted too much from this film.  Renate Reinsve (SENTIMENTAL VALUE) shines as the mother. Recommended

title: WORDS OF LOVE
body: Seven year old Abigail and her mum are outside an apartment building trying to get the attention of the third floor tenant who does not answer the intercom.  The girl wants to meet her father, a man that deserted them before she was born.  After the intervention of the building’s concierge, the third floor window opens and Abigail catches a brief glimpse of him before he slams the window shut.  Unable to accept that her father does not want to be part of her life, Abigail begins an obsessive campaign to change this.  The single mother, (Hafsia Herzi, terrific), is supportive but is also struggling to raise Abigail’s younger half brother, Yoni.  Seven years on, Abigail (she and Yoni now played by different actors) is still trying to connect with her dad but now the overweight Yoni is being bullied at school.  Even their adorable dog cannot console her.  There is not a false note or sentimentality in Rudi Rosenberg’s hidden gem that manages to inject moments of gentle humour amid the pathos.  (Netflix is a coproducer.)  Highly recommended
